subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: (a) Define education and explain the aims of education. (5 marks) (b) Explain the traditional philosophies of education – idealism, naturalism, pragmatism and realism – with their implications for nursing education. (10 marks)

diagram.caption: Traditional philosophies of education compared
labels: idealism (mind and ideals; teacher as role model; lecture
naturalism (child and nature; teacher as observer and guide; learning by doing
pragmatism (experience and utility; teacher as facilitator; projects
realism (the real world and science; teacher as expert guide; demonstration
experiments) – all combined eclectically in nursing education

answer_html:
(a) Definition and aims of education (5 marks) Meaning and definitions

  • The word "education" is derived from the Latin educare (to bring up, to nourish) and educere (to lead out, to draw out) – education draws out the potential within a person.
  • Mahatma Gandhi – "By education I mean an all-round drawing out of the best in child and man – body, mind and spirit."
  • John Dewey – education is the development of all those capacities in the individual which will enable him to control his environment and fulfil his possibilities; it is "a process of living and not a preparation for future living".
  • In simple terms, education is a lifelong, purposeful process of bringing about desirable changes in a person's knowledge, skills, attitudes and behaviour so that he or she can live a useful life in society.

Aims of education

  1. Knowledge aim – to acquire knowledge and develop the intellect, understanding and reasoning.
  2. Vocational aim – to prepare the person for a profession or occupation and earning a livelihood (e.g. competent nurses).
  3. Character and moral aim – to build good character, values, discipline, honesty and a sense of duty.
  4. Harmonious (all-round) development – of the physical, intellectual, emotional, social and spiritual aspects of the personality.
  5. Individual aim – to develop each learner's unique talents and potential to the fullest.
  6. Social aim – to prepare the learner to live with others, serve the community and contribute to social progress.
  7. Citizenship aim – to develop responsible, democratic citizens who respect the Constitution and human rights.
  8. Cultural aim – to preserve, transmit and enrich the cultural heritage.
  9. Physical and health aim – to develop health habits and a healthy body.
  10. Self-realisation and spiritual aim – to help the person understand himself and the meaning of life.
  11. Adjustment and lifelong learning – to help the person adapt to a changing world; the National Education Policy 2020 stresses holistic, multidisciplinary, skill-based and value-based education with critical thinking and lifelong learning.

Aims of nursing education – to prepare competent, caring and ethical nurses who can provide evidence-based care in hospitals and communities, think critically, communicate effectively, lead and manage, and continue to learn throughout their careers.

(b) Traditional philosophies of education (10 marks) Philosophy literally means "love of wisdom" (Greek philos – love, sophia – wisdom). Educational philosophy applies philosophical ideas to the aims, content, methods and evaluation of education. Philosophy decides the aims; education is the practical means of achieving them.

1. Idealism

  • Exponents – Plato, Socrates, Hegel; in India, Swami Vivekananda, Rabindranath Tagore, Mahatma Gandhi and Sri Aurobindo.
  • Basic belief – ideas, mind and spirit are more real than matter; truth, beauty and goodness are eternal values.
  • Aims – self-realisation, development of character and moral and spiritual values, cultural transmission.
  • Curriculum – humanities, ethics, religion, literature, history and the cultural heritage, together with science.
  • Methods – lecture, questioning (Socratic method), discussion, reading and reflection.
  • Teacher – central, a role model and guide, a "gardener" who helps the child grow.
  • Discipline – self-discipline through respect for the teacher's personality and ideals.
  • Implications for nursing – emphasis on values, ethics, compassion, dignity of the patient and the teacher as a role model; the code of ethics and moral reasoning in care.
  • Limitation – may neglect the learner's interests and practical skills.

2. Naturalism

  • Exponents – Jean-Jacques Rousseau (Emile), Herbert Spencer, Froebel, Montessori.
  • Basic belief – nature is the ultimate reality; the child is born good; education should follow the natural development, interests and needs of the child.
  • Aims – natural, free and harmonious development; self-expression and preparation for life.
  • Curriculum – based on the child's interests – nature study, science, physical activities, games, practical work.
  • Methods – learning by doing, observation, play, self-learning, direct experience, heuristic (discovery) method.
  • Teacher – a guide and observer in the background, creating a suitable environment.
  • Discipline – natural consequences ("discipline of nature"); no harsh punishment.
  • Implications for nursing – learner-centred teaching, respect for individual differences, learning by doing in skill labs and clinical areas, self-directed learning, freedom with responsibility.
  • Limitation – neglects social and moral values and the role of the teacher; complete freedom may not suit professional education.

3. Pragmatism

  • Exponents – Charles Peirce, William James and John Dewey.
  • Basic belief – truth is what works in practice; reality is changing; knowledge is gained through experience and experimentation.
  • Aims – to prepare learners to solve problems of real life, adjust to a changing society and develop a democratic, social outlook.
  • Curriculum – flexible and activity-centred, based on the needs of the learner and society (utility).
  • Methods – project method (Kilpatrick), problem-solving, experimentation, learning by doing, group work.
  • Teacher – a facilitator, friend and guide who plans experiences.
  • Discipline – social discipline through cooperative activities.
  • Implications for nursing – problem-based learning, nursing process, case studies, projects, community-based learning, evidence-based practice and adapting care to changing situations.
  • Limitation – no fixed values; too much emphasis on utility.

4. Realism

  • Exponents – Aristotle, John Locke, Comenius, Bertrand Russell.
  • Basic belief – the physical world is real and exists independently of our ideas; knowledge comes through the senses and scientific study.
  • Aims – to prepare the learner for real life, develop the senses, and give scientific and vocational knowledge.
  • Curriculum – sciences, mathematics, practical and vocational subjects.
  • Methods – demonstration, observation, experiments, field trips, audiovisual aids and teaching from simple to complex and concrete to abstract.
  • Teacher – an expert who presents facts objectively.
  • Discipline – based on rules and the realities of life.
  • Implications for nursing – teaching anatomy, physiology and procedures through demonstration, models, specimens, skill labs and clinical exposure; objective evaluation such as OSCE.
  • Limitation – may ignore values, emotions and creativity.

Eclectic approach in nursing education

  • No single philosophy is sufficient. Nursing education combines:
    • Idealism – values and ethics;
    • Naturalism – learner-centred, self-directed learning;
    • Pragmatism – problem-solving and experience-based learning;
    • Realism – scientific knowledge, demonstration and skills.
  • Modern philosophies such as existentialism (freedom, choice, responsibility, meaning – reflected in holistic, person-centred care) and humanism (Carl Rogers, Maslow – the learner's self-actualisation) also influence nursing education.

Relationship between philosophy and education

  • Philosophy and education are two sides of the same coin – philosophy is the theory and education the practice. Philosophy answers the question "why" (aims and values), while education answers "how" (methods and organisation).
  • Every element of education – aims, curriculum, methods, the role of the teacher, discipline, textbooks and evaluation – is shaped by the philosophy accepted by a society or institution. A nursing teacher who understands these philosophies can choose methods consciously rather than by habit.

Conclusion Education is a lifelong process of drawing out a person's potential and bringing about desirable changes in knowledge, skills and attitudes; its aims include knowledge, vocational, character, harmonious, individual, social, citizenship, cultural and spiritual development. Idealism stresses ideals and the teacher as role model, naturalism the child and learning by doing, pragmatism experience and problem-solving, and realism scientific knowledge and demonstration. Nursing education adopts an eclectic blend of these to prepare competent, caring and ethical nurses.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: (a) Define the teaching–learning process and explain its nature and characteristics. (5 marks) (b) Explain the principles of teaching and learning. (6 marks) (c) Describe the barriers to teaching and learning. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: The teaching–learning process
labels: learning style) interacting through content and communication in a learning environment
with evaluation and feedback leading to changed behaviour and replanning

answer_html:
(a) Definition, nature and characteristics (5 marks) Definitions

  • Teaching – a planned, purposeful activity that creates conditions for learning; according to N. L. Gage, teaching is a form of interpersonal influence aimed at changing the behaviour potential of another person.
  • Learning – a relatively permanent change in behaviour that results from practice or experience.
  • Teaching–learning process – a dynamic, interactive and systematic process in which the teacher and learner work together, using content, methods and media in a suitable environment, so that the learner achieves the desired changes in knowledge, skills and attitudes.

Elements

  1. Teacher – knowledge, skills, attitudes, teaching style.
  2. Learner – needs, readiness, motivation, abilities, learning style.
  3. Objectives/learning outcomes – what is to be achieved.
  4. Content – what is to be taught.
  5. Methods and media – how it is to be taught.
  6. Environment – physical, social and psychological.
  7. Evaluation and feedback – how far objectives were achieved.

Nature and characteristics

  • It is a goal-directed process aimed at specific learning outcomes.
  • It is interactive and two-way – teaching and learning influence each other.
  • It is dynamic and continuous; learning goes on throughout life.
  • It is systematic – planning, implementation and evaluation.
  • It is learner-centred in modern education – the teacher is a facilitator.
  • It involves communication – verbal and non-verbal.
  • It covers all three domains – cognitive, affective and psychomotor.
  • It is influenced by many factors – teacher, learner, content, environment.
  • It is both an art and a science – it uses principles and research and also creativity.
  • Evaluation and feedback are built into it; it leads to observable changes in behaviour.

(b) Principles of teaching and learning (6 marks) Principles of teaching

  1. Principle of aim – teaching should have clear objectives.
  2. Principle of planning – lessons should be planned systematically.
  3. Principle of motivation – arouse and sustain the learner's interest.
  4. Principle of activity and participation – learners learn best by doing and participating.
  5. Principle of individual differences – teaching should suit learners' abilities, backgrounds and learning styles.
  6. Principle of linking with life – relate content to real life and clinical practice.
  7. Principle of correlation – link with other subjects (e.g. anatomy with nursing procedures).
  8. Principle of selection and division – select relevant content and divide it into manageable units.
  9. Principle of democratic dealing – respect for learners and freedom to ask questions.
  10. Principle of evaluation and feedback – continuous evaluation and remedial teaching.

Maxims of teaching – proceed from the known to the unknown, simple to complex, concrete to abstract, particular to general, whole to part, observation to reasoning, empirical to rational and psychological to logical.

Principles of learning

  1. Readiness – learning is effective when the learner is physically, mentally and emotionally ready.
  2. Motivation – a motivated learner learns faster and better.
  3. Active participation – learning by doing; involvement of many senses.
  4. Relevance and meaningfulness – meaningful material is learnt and retained better.
  5. Repetition and practice – practice strengthens learning (law of exercise).
  6. Reinforcement and feedback – rewarding correct responses strengthens learning (law of effect); immediate feedback corrects errors.
  7. Learning proceeds step by step from simple to complex.
  8. Primacy and recency – what is learnt first and last is remembered best.
  9. Transfer of learning – learning in one situation helps in another (classroom to clinical area).
  10. Individual differences – each person learns at his or her own pace and style.
  11. Positive learning environment – free from fear and anxiety.

(c) Barriers to teaching and learning (4 marks) Teacher-related

  • Poor knowledge or preparation, unclear objectives, monotonous lecturing, poor communication skills, lack of enthusiasm, authoritarian attitude, favouritism, heavy workload, lack of training in teaching methods. Learner-related

  • Lack of readiness or motivation, poor previous knowledge, language difficulties, anxiety and fear of failure, fatigue (night duties), personal and family problems, health problems, poor study habits, distractions (mobile phones). Content-related – too much content, difficult or irrelevant content, poor sequencing. Environmental

  • Overcrowded classrooms, poor lighting and ventilation, noise, uncomfortable seating, lack of AV aids and internet, lack of clinical facilities. Organisational

  • Rigid timetable, shortage of faculty, heavy curriculum, poor coordination between classroom and clinical teaching, lack of library and skill-lab resources. Communication barriers – jargon, speaking too fast, lack of feedback, cultural and language differences.

Overcoming barriers – clear objectives and good planning, interactive and varied methods, use of media, motivation and positive reinforcement, individual attention and counselling, a comfortable learning environment, faculty development and adequate resources.

Phases of teaching (Philip Jackson)

  1. Pre-active phase (planning) – deciding objectives, analysing learners, selecting content, methods, media and evaluation, and preparing the lesson plan.
  2. Interactive phase (execution) – the actual teaching in class or clinical area: introducing the topic, presenting content, questioning, demonstrating, encouraging participation and giving feedback.
  3. Post-active phase (evaluation) – assessing how far objectives were achieved, reflecting on the lesson and planning remedial teaching or changes.

Levels of teaching

  • Memory level (Herbart) – learning of facts by repetition; thinking is least involved (e.g. normal values of vital signs).
  • Understanding level (Morrison) – learners grasp relationships, principles and meanings and can apply them (e.g. why BP rises in pain).
  • Reflective level (Hunt) – problem-centred, involves critical thinking and independent judgement (e.g. planning care for a patient with several problems). Good teaching moves learners from memory to understanding to reflective level.

Role of the teacher in facilitating learning

  • Planner and organiser of learning experiences; motivator; facilitator who encourages active participation; resource person; role model of professional behaviour; evaluator who gives timely feedback; counsellor who supports learners with difficulties.
  • In nursing, the teacher also links classroom learning with clinical practice through demonstration, supervision and clinical teaching.

Factors influencing the teaching–learning process

  • Learner factors – age, intelligence, previous knowledge, motivation, interest, health, emotional state, learning style, study habits and socio-economic background.
  • Teacher factors – mastery of the subject, teaching skills, personality, enthusiasm, communication, attitude towards learners and ability to use media.
  • Content factors – difficulty, length, meaningfulness and organisation of the material.
  • Method factors – suitability of the method to the objectives, group size and learners; use of active methods and AV aids.
  • Environmental factors – physical facilities (seating, lighting, ventilation, noise), emotional climate (freedom from fear, mutual respect), and availability of library, skill lab and clinical facilities.
  • Time factors – time of day, duration of sessions, spacing of learning and fatigue after night duty.

Conclusion The teaching–learning process is a goal-directed, interactive, dynamic and systematic process between teacher and learner that brings about changes in knowledge, skills and attitudes. It is guided by principles of teaching (aim, planning, motivation, activity, individual differences, linking with life, evaluation) and learning (readiness, motivation, participation, practice, reinforcement, transfer), and can be hindered by teacher, learner, content, environmental, organisational and communication barriers that a good teacher identifies and overcomes.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Define educational technology and explain its approaches and scope.
answer_html:
Definition

  • Educational technology is the systematic application of scientific knowledge about teaching, learning and communication, together with appropriate tools, media and techniques, to design, implement and evaluate the teaching–learning process so that learning becomes more effective and efficient.
  • It is both technology of education (systematic methods of planning, teaching and evaluating) and technology in education (the use of machines and media in teaching).

Approaches

  1. Hardware approach – the use of machines and equipment – projectors, computers, smart boards, audio and video devices, simulators, mobile devices and the internet – to teach more learners, more effectively. It is derived from physical sciences and engineering.
  2. Software approach – the use of principles of psychology of learning to develop teaching materials and techniques – programmed instruction, instructional objectives, teaching strategies, lesson design, e-content, evaluation tools. It gives the "content" that runs on the hardware.
  3. Systems approach – treats education as a system with inputs (learners, teachers, curriculum, resources), processes (teaching–learning activities) and outputs (competent graduates), with feedback to improve the system. It involves analysis of needs, setting objectives, selecting methods and media, implementation, evaluation and revision.

Scope of educational technology

  • Determining aims and objectives – writing learning outcomes in behavioural terms.
  • Curriculum design and development.
  • Analysis of learners' needs and characteristics.
  • Development of teaching strategies and methods – including microteaching, programmed learning, simulation and active learning.
  • Development and use of media – AV aids, e-content, multimedia, virtual reality.
  • Management of the teaching–learning environment – classroom, skill lab, clinical area, online platforms.
  • Evaluation – construction of tests, OSCE, item analysis, feedback mechanisms.
  • Distance and open learning – online courses and blended programmes.
  • Teacher training – faculty development in teaching skills.
  • Research in teaching and learning.

Importance in nursing education – allows standardised, safe practice through simulation and skill labs; supports large classes and distance learning; makes teaching interesting and learner-centred; and enables objective assessment of competencies.

Forms of educational technology – teaching technology (planning, organising, leading and controlling the teaching activity), instructional technology (presenting content through media and programmed instruction) and behavioural technology (modifying the behaviour of the teacher and learner, e.g. through microteaching and interaction analysis).

Conclusion Educational technology is the systematic application of knowledge, methods and media to improve teaching and learning. Its hardware, software and systems approaches together cover objectives, curriculum, strategies, media, environment, evaluation, distance learning, teacher training and research.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the latest approaches to education – transformational, relationship-based and competency-based education.
answer_html:
1. Transformational (transformative) education

  • Based on Jack Mezirow's transformative learning theory – learning that changes the way a person thinks, feels and sees the world (frames of reference), not just what he or she knows.
  • Process – a disorienting dilemma (e.g. a student's first experience of a dying patient) → critical reflection on assumptions → discussion with others → exploring new roles → building confidence → reintegrating a new perspective into life.
  • Teaching strategies – reflective journals, critical incident analysis, case discussions, simulation with debriefing, community postings, dialogue and storytelling.
  • Teacher's role – creating a safe environment, asking challenging questions, encouraging reflection.
  • In nursing – develops critical thinking, empathy, professional identity and leadership, preparing nurses to change practice and society.

2. Relationship-based education

  • Recognises that learning happens through relationships – between teacher and student, among students, and with patients and the community.
  • Key elements – trust, respect, caring, empathy, open communication, mutual responsibility and a sense of belonging.
  • Practices – mentoring and preceptorship, small-group learning, regular feedback, knowing students as individuals, being available, modelling caring behaviour.
  • In nursing – students who are cared for learn to care for others; good student–faculty relationships reduce anxiety, improve motivation and retention, and support professional socialisation.

3. Competency-based education (CBE)

  • An outcome-based approach in which the curriculum is designed around the competencies (integrated knowledge, skills, attitudes and values) a graduate must demonstrate in practice.
  • Features
    • Clearly defined competencies and learning outcomes derived from the roles of the nurse.
    • Learner-centred, with emphasis on demonstration of performance rather than time spent.
    • Integration of theory and practice; skill labs and simulation before clinical practice.
    • Continuous, workplace-based assessment using direct observation, checklists, OSCE, logbooks, portfolios and competency checklists (Miller's pyramid – knows, knows how, shows how, does).
    • Constructive feedback and remediation until competence is achieved.
  • The INC B.Sc Nursing curriculum (2021) is competency-based – it defines programme outcomes and competencies, includes mandatory skill-lab practice, clinical competency lists and logbooks.
  • Advantages – produces practice-ready nurses, clear expectations, objective assessment, accountability.
  • Challenges – needs trained faculty, more resources (skill labs, simulators), time-consuming assessment and a change in teachers' mindset.

Conclusion Transformational education changes learners' perspectives through critical reflection; relationship-based education uses caring, trusting relationships as the foundation of learning; and competency-based education focuses on demonstrable outcomes assessed in practice – together they shape modern nursing education, including the INC 2021 curriculum.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain simulation-based learning in nursing education.
answer_html:
Definition Simulation-based learning is a teaching strategy in which learners practise realistic clinical situations in a safe, controlled environment using manikins, models, simulated patients or computers, followed by guided reflection (debriefing). It replaces or amplifies real experiences without risk to patients.

Types

  1. By fidelity (degree of realism)
    • Low fidelity – static models and part-task trainers (injection pad, IV arm, catheterisation model, CPR manikin).
    • Medium fidelity – manikins with heart and breath sounds, pulses.
    • High fidelity – computerised manikins that breathe, talk, blink, show changing vital signs and respond to interventions (e.g. a deteriorating patient, PPH simulator).
  2. Standardised (simulated) patients – trained actors or peers who portray patients for communication, history-taking and counselling practice.
  3. Virtual and screen-based simulation – computer programs, virtual reality, serious games.
  4. Hybrid simulation – a standardised patient combined with a task trainer (e.g. an actor wearing a birthing simulator).
  5. In-situ simulation – conducted in the real ward or emergency department with the actual team.

Phases of a simulation session

  1. Prebriefing – orientation to the environment and equipment, objectives, roles and a "safe container" agreement (mistakes are part of learning, confidentiality).
  2. Scenario (simulation activity) – students perform care in a realistic case (e.g. a post-operative patient going into shock) while the facilitator controls the scenario and observes.
  3. Debriefing – the most important phase; a structured reflective discussion – what happened, how they felt, what went well, what could be improved and how it applies to practice (e.g. using the plus–delta or "gather–analyse–summarise" approach).
  4. Evaluation – of learners' performance and of the simulation itself.

Advantages

  • Patient safety – students learn and make mistakes without harming patients.
  • Practice of rare and high-risk situations (cardiac arrest, eclampsia, PPH, neonatal resuscitation).
  • Repeated practice to mastery; standardised experiences for all students.
  • Develops clinical reasoning, decision-making, teamwork, communication and confidence.
  • Immediate feedback; allows objective assessment (e.g. in OSCE).
  • Bridges the gap between theory and clinical practice.

Limitations

  • High cost of high-fidelity equipment and maintenance; need for trained facilitators and technical staff.
  • Time-consuming; small groups only.
  • Cannot fully replace real patient contact; some students feel anxious or treat it as "unreal".

Role of the teacher – writes scenarios linked to learning outcomes, prepares the environment and equipment, facilitates and observes without interrupting, conducts structured debriefing, gives constructive feedback and evaluates.

Conclusion Simulation-based learning lets nursing students practise realistic situations safely, using low- to high-fidelity manikins, standardised patients, virtual and hybrid simulation, through prebriefing, scenario and debriefing; it improves skills, reasoning, teamwork and confidence, although it needs resources and trained facilitators.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the philosophy of nursing education.
answer_html:
Meaning A philosophy of nursing education is a statement of beliefs and values about nursing, health, the learner, the teacher and the educational process, which guides the aims, curriculum, teaching methods and evaluation of a nursing programme.

Beliefs expressed in the INC philosophy for B.Sc Nursing (summarised)

  • Health is a state of physical, mental, social and spiritual well-being and a basic right; nursing contributes to the health of individuals, families and communities.
  • Nursing is a profession that combines science and art, based on a body of knowledge, ethics and values, providing holistic, compassionate and culturally sensitive care across the life span and in all settings.
  • Nursing education should be competency-based and learner-centred, integrating theory with practice through skill labs, simulation and clinical experience.
  • It should prepare nurses who are critical thinkers, evidence-based practitioners, effective communicators, team members, leaders and managers, able to work in hospitals and communities and respond to the health needs of the country.
  • Education is a lifelong process; graduates should be motivated for continuing education and professional development.
  • Ethics, values, professionalism and accountability are integral to nursing.
  • Faculty are facilitators and role models; the learning environment should encourage self-directed learning, inquiry and creativity.

Institutional philosophy – every nursing college writes its own philosophy in line with INC and the university, describing its beliefs about the student, faculty, community and the kind of nurse it wants to prepare.

Components of a philosophy statement – beliefs about human beings, health, nursing, the learner, the teacher, the learning environment, society and education.

Importance

  • Gives direction to aims, objectives and curriculum.
  • Ensures consistency among faculty in teaching and evaluation.
  • Guides selection of students, methods, clinical experiences and evaluation.
  • Provides a basis for evaluating the programme.
  • Develops a shared professional identity and values.

Example of an institutional philosophy statement – "We believe that every student is a unique individual with the potential to become a competent, compassionate and ethical nurse. Learning is a lifelong, active process best achieved when theory is integrated with practice in a supportive environment, and the teacher acts as a facilitator, mentor and role model."

Conclusion The philosophy of nursing education expresses beliefs about health, nursing, the learner and education – in INC's view, competency-based, learner-centred, holistic, ethical and evidence-based preparation of nurses for lifelong learning and service – and gives direction and consistency to the entire programme.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain experiential learning and reflective learning in nursing education.
answer_html:
1. Experiential learning

  • Meaning – learning through direct experience followed by reflection – "learning by doing and thinking about what was done".
  • David Kolb's experiential learning cycle (1984) has four stages:
    1. Concrete experience – the learner has an experience (e.g. giving a bed bath to a patient for the first time).
    2. Reflective observation – reviews and reflects on the experience (what happened, how the patient responded).
    3. Abstract conceptualisation – draws conclusions and links them with theory (principles of hygiene and dignity).
    4. Active experimentation – tries out the new learning in the next situation, leading to a new experience.
  • Kolb also described learning styles – diverging, assimilating, converging and accommodating.
  • Strategies – clinical practice, skill labs, simulation, role play, field visits, community postings, projects, service learning.

2. Reflective learning

  • Meaning – learning by thinking critically about one's experiences, feelings and actions to understand them and improve future practice.
  • Donald Schön described reflection-in-action (thinking while doing) and reflection-on-action (thinking after the event).
  • Gibbs' reflective cycle (1988) – six stages:
    1. Description – what happened?
    2. Feelings – what was I thinking and feeling?
    3. Evaluation – what was good and bad about the experience?
    4. Analysis – what sense can I make of it?
    5. Conclusion – what else could I have done?
    6. Action plan – what will I do if it happens again?
  • Strategies – reflective journals and diaries, critical incident analysis, debriefing after simulation and clinical shifts, portfolios, group reflection sessions.

Advantages

  • Integrates theory with practice; makes learning meaningful and lasting.
  • Develops critical thinking, clinical judgement, self-awareness, empathy and professional identity.
  • Encourages lifelong, self-directed learning and continuous improvement of practice.
  • Helps students cope with emotional experiences (death of a patient, errors).

Role of the teacher – provides suitable experiences, guides reflection with open questions, gives feedback on journals, maintains confidentiality and creates a non-judgemental atmosphere.

Example of a reflective journal entry (brief) – "Today my patient refused his insulin injection. I felt nervous and annoyed. When I sat with him, I learned that he feared hypoglycaemia after a previous episode. I explained the signs and showed him how to check his sugar. Next time I will first ask about the patient's fears before insisting on the procedure."

Conclusion Experiential learning (Kolb's cycle of experience, reflection, conceptualisation and experimentation) and reflective learning (Schön's reflection-in- and on-action, Gibbs' six-stage cycle) help nursing students learn deeply from practice and become thoughtful, self-improving professionals.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: What is blended learning?
answer_html:
Blended learning is an approach that combines face-to-face classroom teaching with online (e-learning) activities, so that learners get the benefits of both.

  • Examples – lectures and skill-lab sessions in college plus online videos, quizzes, discussion forums and assignments through a learning management system; the flipped classroom, in which students study the material online before class and use class time for discussion and problem-solving. Advantages

  • Flexibility of time and place; self-paced learning.

  • Better student engagement and active learning.
  • Wider access to resources; efficient use of class time.
  • Develops digital skills. Requirements – internet access, devices, well-designed e-content and trained teachers.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: What is scenario-based learning?
answer_html:
Scenario-based learning is a teaching strategy in which students learn by working through realistic, story-based situations (scenarios) that they are likely to meet in practice, making decisions and solving problems.

  • Example – "A 60-year-old man, two days after abdominal surgery, becomes restless with a pulse of 120 per minute and BP of 90/60 mmHg – what will you do?"
  • Scenarios may be paper-based, video-based, computer-based (branching scenarios) or used in simulation. Advantages – develops clinical reasoning, decision-making and problem-solving, links theory with practice, prepares students for real situations and can be used for both teaching and assessment.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: List the maxims of teaching.
answer_html:
Maxims of teaching are general rules that make teaching effective:

  1. From known to unknown – start with what students already know.
  2. From simple to complex.
  3. From concrete to abstract – use real objects and examples before theory.
  4. From particular to general – examples first, then rules (induction).
  5. From whole to part – give an overview, then details.
  6. From analysis to synthesis.
  7. From observation to reasoning.
  8. From empirical to rational – experience first, then explanation.
  9. From psychological to logical – according to the learner's interest, then logical order. Example – teaching blood pressure measurement by first recalling pulse measurement (known), demonstrating on a student (concrete), then explaining the physiology (abstract).

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: (a) Define curriculum and list its types. (3 marks) (b) Explain the components and approaches of curriculum design. (4 marks) (c) Describe the process of curriculum development, with its influencing factors, facilitators and barriers. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Curriculum development cycle
labels: situation and needs analysis – philosophy and aims – learning outcomes – selection and organisation of content – selection and organisation of learning experiences – evaluation methods – implementation – evaluation and revision
feeding back to needs analysis (Wheeler's cyclical model)

answer_html:
(a) Definition and types (3 marks) Definition

  • The word curriculum comes from the Latin currere, meaning "to run" – a race course; it is the course which students run to reach their goal.
  • Hilda Taba described curriculum as a plan for learning.
  • Commonly, curriculum is the sum total of all the learning experiences – in the classroom, laboratory, clinical area and community – that are planned, organised and guided by an educational institution to achieve its educational goals.
  • In nursing, the curriculum (for example, the INC B.Sc Nursing curriculum, 2021) describes the philosophy, aims, programme outcomes, courses, content, hours, teaching–learning methods, clinical experiences and evaluation of the programme.

Types of curriculum

  1. Subject-centred curriculum – organised around separate subjects (anatomy, physiology, nursing foundations).
  2. Learner-centred (child-centred) curriculum – based on the needs, interests and abilities of learners.
  3. Problem-centred (core) curriculum – organised around real-life problems (e.g. problem-based learning).
  4. Activity or experience curriculum – learning through activities and experiences.
  5. Integrated curriculum – related subjects are combined around themes (horizontal and vertical integration).
  6. Competency-based curriculum – built around competencies to be demonstrated (as in INC 2021).
  7. Spiral curriculum (Jerome Bruner) – topics are revisited at increasing levels of depth across years.
  8. Core curriculum – essential content that all students must learn.
  9. Hidden curriculum – values and behaviours learnt informally from the institution's culture.
  10. Null curriculum – what is deliberately or unintentionally not taught.
  11. Formal and informal curriculum – planned courses versus co-curricular activities.

(b) Components and approaches of curriculum design (4 marks) Components (elements)

  1. Philosophy and aims – beliefs about health, nursing, learners and education.
  2. Objectives/learning outcomes – what the graduate should know, do and value.
  3. Content (subject matter) – selected for validity, significance, relevance, utility and learnability, and organised according to:
    • scope – breadth and depth;
    • sequence – order, from simple to complex;
    • continuity – repetition and reinforcement of key elements;
    • integration – links across subjects;
    • balance – between theory and practice and among subjects.
  4. Learning experiences (teaching–learning methods) – lectures, demonstrations, skill-lab practice, clinical postings, community experience, projects, simulation.
  5. Resources – faculty, time, clinical facilities, library, laboratories, media.
  6. Evaluation – formative and summative assessment of students and evaluation of the programme.

Approaches to curriculum design

  • Subject-centred design – emphasis on content of disciplines.
  • Learner-centred design – emphasis on learners' needs and active learning.
  • Problem-centred design – organised around health problems or life situations.
  • Competency-based/outcome-based design – starts with the competencies or outcomes and works backwards to content and methods ("backward design").
  • Systems approach – curriculum as a system of inputs, processes, outputs and feedback.
  • Integrated and spiral approaches – horizontal integration (subjects taught together in a semester), vertical integration (basic and clinical subjects linked across years) and spiral revisiting of topics.

(c) Process of curriculum development (8 marks) Models

  • Ralph Tyler (1949) – four fundamental questions:
    • What educational purposes should the school seek to attain? (objectives)
    • What learning experiences can be provided to attain these purposes? (experiences)
    • How can these experiences be effectively organised? (organisation)
    • How can we determine whether the purposes are being attained? (evaluation)
  • Hilda Taba (1962) – a "grassroots" model in which teachers participate, with seven steps:
    1. diagnosis of needs;
    2. formulation of objectives;
    3. selection of content;
    4. organisation of content;
    5. selection of learning experiences;
    6. organisation of learning experiences;
    7. determination of what to evaluate and how.
  • D. K. Wheeler (1967) – a cyclical model in which evaluation feeds back into the next cycle of planning.

Steps in curriculum development

  1. Formation of a curriculum committee – principal, faculty from all specialties, students, clinical partners, community representatives and experts.
  2. Situation and needs analysis
    • Health needs and problems of the community; disease patterns and demographic changes.
    • National health policies and programmes (National Health Policy, NEP 2020).
    • Requirements of the regulatory bodies (INC, State Nursing Council and university).
    • Characteristics of learners (entry qualification, age, background).
    • Available resources – faculty, hospitals, community areas, finances; review of the existing curriculum and feedback from graduates and employers.
  3. Formulation of philosophy and aims of the programme.
  4. Writing programme outcomes and course objectives/competencies in measurable terms.
  5. Selection of content – relevant, up to date, evidence-based and appropriate to the level of learners.
  6. Organisation of content – into courses, units and topics; deciding sequence, credits and hours; preparing a master plan (year-wise and semester-wise distribution) and clinical rotation plans.
  7. Selection and organisation of learning experiences – classroom methods, skill labs, simulation, clinical and community postings, self-directed learning, electives.
  8. Planning evaluation – internal assessment, university examinations, clinical evaluation tools, competency checklists and programme evaluation methods.
  9. Implementation – orientation of faculty and students, preparation of course plans, unit plans and lesson plans, arranging resources; sometimes a pilot implementation.
  10. Evaluation and revision – continuous feedback from students, faculty, clinical staff and employers; examination results; periodic revision to keep the curriculum relevant.

Factors influencing curriculum development

  • Philosophical – beliefs and values of society and the profession.
  • Social and cultural – needs, values and expectations of the community; gender and cultural diversity.
  • Health care needs and system – disease burden, health programmes, shift to primary health care and Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.
  • Professional and regulatory – INC and university regulations, scope of nursing practice, accreditation (NAAC).
  • Scientific and technological advances – new knowledge, simulation, digital health.
  • Learners – abilities, interests, previous education, generation characteristics.
  • Faculty – number, qualifications and expertise.
  • Economic and political – funding, government policies, employment opportunities.
  • Global trends – international standards, migration of nurses, competency-based education.

Facilitators

  • Supportive leadership and administration; committed, trained faculty working as a team.
  • Participation of students, clinical partners and the community.
  • Adequate resources – time, funds, clinical areas, skill labs, library.
  • Clear guidelines from regulatory bodies; availability of model curricula.
  • Good communication, research evidence and regular evaluation data.

Barriers

  • Resistance to change among faculty and administrators; preference for traditional methods.
  • Lack of time, heavy teaching and clinical workload.
  • Shortage of qualified faculty and lack of training in curriculum development.
  • Inadequate resources – skill labs, simulators, clinical placements.
  • Rigid regulations, centralised examinations, large student numbers.
  • Poor coordination between college and hospital; lack of feedback mechanisms.

Role of the nurse educator – serves on the curriculum committee, contributes to needs analysis, writes course objectives, plans content and learning experiences, prepares teaching plans, implements and evaluates the curriculum and gives feedback for revision.

Conclusion Curriculum is the planned set of learning experiences that leads students to their educational goals; it may be subject-, learner-, problem-, competency-based, integrated or spiral, and its design includes philosophy, objectives, content, learning experiences, resources and evaluation. Curriculum development, guided by models such as Tyler's, Taba's and Wheeler's, proceeds from needs analysis through objectives, content, learning experiences and evaluation to implementation and revision, influenced by social, professional, scientific and economic factors, helped by leadership and resources, and hindered by resistance, workload and lack of resources.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: (a) Define learning outcomes (behavioural objectives) and state their purposes and characteristics. (4 marks) (b) Explain Bloom's taxonomy of educational objectives with examples. (7 marks) (c) Describe the guidelines for writing learning outcomes. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Bloom's taxonomy – three domains
labels: each arranged as a staircase from simple to complex

answer_html:
(a) Definition, purposes and characteristics (4 marks) Definition

  • A learning outcome (behavioural or instructional objective) is a clear statement of what the learner will be able to know, do or value at the end of a period of learning, expressed in terms of observable and measurable behaviour.
  • General objectives state broad goals of a course or unit (e.g. "the student will understand the care of patients with diabetes").
  • Specific (behavioural) objectives state precise, measurable behaviour (e.g. "the student will demonstrate subcutaneous insulin injection correctly on a manikin").

Purposes

  1. Guide the teacher in selecting content, methods, media and evaluation.
  2. Guide the learner – tell students what is expected and help them organise their study.
  3. Provide a basis for evaluation – tests are constructed to measure the stated objectives.
  4. Communicate the intent of the course to students, other teachers, administrators and employers.
  5. Ensure consistency among teachers teaching the same course.
  6. Help in curriculum planning and in identifying gaps.
  7. Motivate learners through clear targets.

Characteristics of good objectives (SMART)

  • Specific – one clear behaviour, not vague.
  • Measurable – observable action verbs such as "list", "explain", "demonstrate".
  • Achievable – realistic for the learners' level and time.
  • Relevant – related to the course and the nurse's role.
  • Time-bound – achievable by a stated time (end of the session or unit).
  • Also: learner-centred ("the student will…"), stated in terms of outcome, not teaching activity, and covering all three domains.

(b) Bloom's taxonomy (7 marks) Benjamin Bloom (1956) and colleagues classified educational objectives into three domains, each arranged in a hierarchy from simple to complex.

1. Cognitive domain (knowledge and intellectual skills) The original levels were knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis and evaluation. The revised taxonomy (Anderson and Krathwohl, 2001) uses verbs:

  1. Remember – recall facts. Verbs: define, list, name, state. Example: "List the normal values of vital signs."
  2. Understand – explain ideas. Verbs: explain, describe, classify, summarise. Example: "Explain the causes of hypovolaemic shock."
  3. Apply – use knowledge in a new situation. Verbs: calculate, use, demonstrate, solve. Example: "Calculate the IV flow rate for a prescribed infusion."
  4. Analyse – break information into parts and find relationships. Verbs: differentiate, compare, analyse. Example: "Differentiate between type 1 and type 2 diabetes."
  5. Evaluate – make judgements using criteria. Verbs: judge, justify, prioritise, critique. Example: "Prioritise the nursing diagnoses of a post-operative patient."
  6. Create – put elements together into a new whole. Verbs: plan, design, develop, formulate. Example: "Plan a health education session for diabetic patients."

2. Affective domain (attitudes, values, feelings) – Krathwohl, Bloom and Masia (1964)

  1. Receiving – willingness to listen and pay attention. Example: "Listens attentively to a patient's concerns."
  2. Responding – active participation. Example: "Answers the patient's questions politely."
  3. Valuing – attaching worth to an idea or behaviour. Example: "Shows respect for the privacy of patients."
  4. Organisation – bringing values together and resolving conflicts. Example: "Balances professional duties with personal beliefs when caring for patients."
  5. Characterisation by a value – consistent behaviour reflecting a value system. Example: "Consistently practises ethical, compassionate care."

3. Psychomotor domain (motor skills) – classified by Simpson (1972) and Dave (1970)

  • Simpson's levels – perception (awareness of cues), set (readiness to act), guided response (imitation and trial and error under guidance), mechanism (habitual performance with confidence), complex overt response (skilful, accurate performance), adaptation (modifying skills for new situations) and origination (creating new movement patterns).
  • Dave's levels – imitation, manipulation, precision, articulation and naturalisation.
  • Example: "Performs nasogastric tube insertion following all steps of the procedure under supervision" (guided response) → "Performs it independently and adapts the technique for a restless patient" (adaptation).

Importance – the taxonomy helps teachers write objectives at different levels, avoid over-emphasis on recall, plan suitable methods (lectures for knowledge, demonstration and practice for skills, discussion and role play for attitudes) and set balanced examinations.

(c) Guidelines for writing learning outcomes (4 marks)

  1. Start with the learner – "At the end of the session, the student will be able to…".
  2. Use one action verb that describes observable behaviour; avoid vague verbs such as "know", "understand", "appreciate", "learn".
  3. State one outcome per objective.
  4. Use the ABCD method:
    • A – Audience – who will perform (the second-year B.Sc Nursing student).
    • B – Behaviour – what the learner will do (measure blood pressure).
    • C – Condition – under what circumstances (using a sphygmomanometer on an adult patient).
    • D – Degree – the standard of performance (with an accuracy of ±4 mmHg compared with the teacher's reading).
    • Complete example: "The second-year student will measure the blood pressure of an adult patient using a sphygmomanometer with an accuracy of ±4 mmHg."
  5. Cover all three domains and different levels of the hierarchy.
  6. Make them realistic for the time and level of learners.
  7. Align objectives with content, teaching methods and assessment (constructive alignment).
  8. Write clinical learning outcomes in terms of patient care, e.g. "The student will provide pre-operative care to an assigned patient following the hospital checklist."

Common errors in writing objectives

  • Using vague, non-measurable verbs – "know", "understand", "appreciate", "be aware of".
  • Describing the teacher's activity instead of the learner's behaviour ("to teach the students about asepsis").
  • Writing two or more behaviours in one objective ("list and explain…").
  • Stating content topics instead of outcomes ("anatomy of the heart").
  • Writing objectives only at the lowest cognitive level (recall) and neglecting affective and psychomotor domains.
  • Setting objectives that are unrealistic for the time or level of students.

Example – set of specific objectives for a session on "Oxygen administration" At the end of the session, the second-year students will be able to:

  1. Define oxygen therapy (cognitive – remember).
  2. Explain the indications and hazards of oxygen therapy (cognitive – understand).
  3. Calculate the flow rate for a prescribed concentration using a Venturi mask (cognitive – apply).
  4. Demonstrate oxygen administration by nasal cannula on a manikin following the checklist (psychomotor).
  5. Explain the procedure to the patient with respect and reassurance (affective – responding).

Programme outcomes, course outcomes and session outcomes – learning outcomes are written at different levels. Programme outcomes describe what a B.Sc Nursing graduate will be able to do at the end of four years (e.g. provide safe, evidence-based care across settings). Course outcomes describe the end result of one course, and session (specific) objectives describe what will be achieved in one class. Each level should support the level above it, so that every lesson contributes to the competencies of the graduate nurse.

Conclusion Learning outcomes are clear, learner-centred statements of measurable behaviour that guide teaching, learning and evaluation and should be SMART. Bloom's taxonomy classifies them into cognitive (remember to create), affective (receiving to characterisation) and psychomotor (Simpson's perception to origination) domains, and outcomes are best written with one action verb using the ABCD method, aligned with content and assessment.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the lesson plan – its purposes, principles and components.
answer_html:
Definition A lesson plan is a written, step-by-step plan prepared by the teacher for a single teaching session, stating what will be taught, how, with what aids and how learning will be evaluated. It is a teacher's "road map" for the class.

Purposes

  • Gives clear direction and makes teaching systematic and purposeful.
  • Ensures proper selection and sequencing of content within the time.
  • Helps in choosing suitable methods and AV aids.
  • Builds the teacher's confidence and avoids omissions and repetition.
  • Provides a basis for evaluation and for continuity when a substitute teacher takes the class.
  • Serves as a record for future use and improvement.

Principles

  • Based on clear, specific objectives.
  • Considers learners' previous knowledge, needs and level.
  • Follows the maxims of teaching (known to unknown, simple to complex).
  • Includes learner participation and suitable methods.
  • Is flexible, allowing changes during the class.
  • Allots realistic time to each part.
  • Includes evaluation and feedback.

Components (format)

  1. General information – name of the teacher, subject, unit, topic, group (year/semester), number of students, date, time, duration, place and method of teaching.
  2. General objective – broad aim of the lesson.
  3. Specific objectives – measurable outcomes in all three domains.
  4. Previous knowledge of students assumed by the teacher.
  5. AV aids to be used.
  6. Introduction (motivation) – arousing interest through a question, story, case or picture.
  7. Body of the lesson – presented in columns: time, specific objective, content, teaching–learning activities (teacher's and students' activities), AV aids and evaluation for each part.
  8. Summary/recapitulation – key points restated.
  9. Evaluation – questions, quizzes or return demonstration at the end.
  10. Assignment – reading or written work.
  11. References – books and articles used.

Herbartian steps (sequence of presentation) – preparation (introduction), presentation (development of the lesson), comparison and association, generalisation, application and recapitulation.

Qualities of a good lesson plan – clear objectives; appropriate, accurate and up-to-date content; logical sequence; variety of methods and aids; active participation; realistic time; built-in evaluation; flexibility; neat and complete.

Example (brief) – Topic: "Hand hygiene" for first-year students, 45 minutes. Specific objective: students will demonstrate the six steps of hand washing. Introduction: showing a culture plate of organisms from unwashed hands. Development: explanation of the indications ("five moments"), demonstration, return demonstration by students. Evaluation: observing each student with a checklist.

Conclusion A lesson plan is the teacher's written plan for one session, prepared on principles of clear objectives, learners' previous knowledge, logical sequence, participation and evaluation; it includes general information, objectives, previous knowledge, AV aids, introduction, content with time and activities, summary, evaluation, assignment and references.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the essential qualities of a good teacher.
answer_html:
Introduction The success of education depends largely on the teacher. A good nursing teacher not only teaches knowledge and skills but also shapes the values, attitudes and professional identity of future nurses.

1. Personal qualities

  • Pleasant personality – cheerful, well-groomed, approachable, with a sense of humour.
  • Good physical and mental health, emotional stability and self-control.
  • Patience, tolerance, empathy and kindness towards students.
  • Honesty, integrity, punctuality and discipline.
  • Enthusiasm for teaching and the profession; creativity and resourcefulness.
  • Fairness and impartiality – no favouritism; respect for every student.
  • Confidence and decisiveness.

2. Professional and intellectual qualities

  • Mastery of the subject – sound, updated knowledge and its application.
  • Clinical competence – able to demonstrate skills and guide students in clinical areas.
  • Teaching skills – planning lessons, using varied methods (lecture, demonstration, discussion, simulation, PBL), using AV aids and technology, managing the class, motivating and questioning.
  • Communication skills – clear speech, good listening, effective non-verbal communication, ability to explain complex ideas simply.
  • Evaluation skills – constructing fair tests, giving constructive feedback.
  • Commitment to lifelong learning – continuing education, higher qualifications, reading journals, attending workshops.
  • Research-mindedness – evidence-based teaching and practice; guiding student projects.
  • Ethical and professional conduct – follows the code of ethics; maintains confidentiality; acts as a role model.

3. Social qualities

  • Good interpersonal relationships with students, colleagues, hospital staff and the community.
  • Leadership and teamwork; ability to work with the curriculum committee and administration.
  • Guidance and counselling ability – understands students' problems and helps them.
  • Cultural sensitivity and respect for diversity.
  • Community-mindedness – involvement in health activities.

4. Qualities specific to the nurse teacher

  • Integrates theory with practice; supervises safely in clinical areas.
  • Balances patient safety with students' learning.
  • Demonstrates caring behaviour towards patients and students.
  • Encourages critical thinking and independence.

What students value most – teachers who explain clearly, are approachable and fair, respect them, give timely and constructive feedback, show enthusiasm, link theory with real patients and support them during difficulties in the clinical area.

Conclusion A good teacher combines personal qualities (pleasant personality, patience, honesty, enthusiasm, fairness), professional qualities (subject mastery, clinical competence, teaching, communication and evaluation skills, lifelong learning, research and ethics) and social qualities (good relationships, leadership, guidance and cultural sensitivity), serving as a role model for future nurses.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the teaching styles – formal authority, demonstrator, facilitator and delegator.
answer_html:
Introduction A teaching style is the characteristic way in which a teacher teaches – the teacher's preferred methods, behaviour and relationship with learners. Anthony Grasha (1996) described five teaching styles: expert, formal authority, personal model (demonstrator), facilitator and delegator. Most teachers use a blend, choosing according to learners and content.

1. Formal authority style

  • Features – teacher-centred; the teacher focuses on content, rules, standards and correct ways of doing things; clear expectations and structured lectures.
  • Advantages – clear goals and expectations; suitable for large groups and for teaching standards, policies and procedures.
  • Disadvantages – rigid; may discourage student participation and creativity.
  • Use – first-year students, regulations, safety rules.

2. Demonstrator (personal model) style

  • Features – the teacher shows how to do things and acts as a role model; students observe and imitate, with coaching and guidance.
  • Advantages – excellent for teaching skills and professional behaviour; students learn by example.
  • Disadvantages – students may copy without understanding; some may feel inadequate if they cannot match the teacher.
  • Use – procedures in skill labs and clinical areas; communication with patients.

3. Facilitator style

  • Features – learner-centred; the teacher guides and supports students to find answers themselves through questions, discussion, problem-solving and projects; emphasises personal flexibility and the teacher–student relationship.
  • Advantages – develops critical thinking, independence and self-directed learning; increases motivation.
  • Disadvantages – time-consuming; may make anxious students uncomfortable if they want direct answers.
  • Use – PBL, case discussions, seminars, clinical conferences.

4. Delegator style

  • Features – the teacher gives responsibility to students to work independently or in groups, acting as a consultant and resource person.
  • Advantages – develops autonomy, leadership and teamwork; suitable for capable, mature learners.
  • Disadvantages – some students may not be ready; the teacher may lose track of progress; risk of misunderstanding.
  • Use – research projects, community surveys, group assignments for senior students.

5. Expert style – the teacher displays detailed knowledge and challenges students to improve their competence; may intimidate beginners.

Choosing a teaching style – depends on learners' level and readiness, the nature of content (knowledge, skill or attitude), group size, time and setting. Early in training, more formal authority and demonstration are needed; later, facilitation and delegation build independence.

Conclusion Teaching styles range from teacher-centred formal authority and demonstrator styles to learner-centred facilitator and delegator styles. A good nurse teacher blends them – setting standards, demonstrating skills, facilitating thinking and delegating responsibility – according to learners and content.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the determinants of learning – learning needs, readiness to learn and learning styles.
answer_html:
Introduction Effective teaching starts with assessing the learner. Three major determinants of learning are the learner's needs, readiness and learning style.

1. Learning needs

  • Meaning – the gap between what the learner already knows or can do and what he or she needs to know or do (the desired competence).
  • Methods of assessment
    • Pre-tests and quizzes; questioning at the start of a session.
    • Observation of performance in skill labs and clinical areas.
    • Discussion with learners, self-assessment questionnaires and focus groups.
    • Review of previous records, examination results and curriculum requirements.
    • Feedback from clinical staff.
  • Prioritising needs – essential for safe practice first ("need to know"), then "nice to know".

2. Readiness to learn

  • Meaning – the state of being physically, mentally and emotionally prepared to learn; Thorndike's law of readiness states that learning is satisfying when the learner is ready.
  • Types (PEEK)
    • Physical readiness – health, energy, freedom from pain and fatigue (e.g. after night duty, students are less ready).
    • Emotional readiness – motivation, anxiety level, interest and attitude.
    • Experiential readiness – past experiences and culture that influence learning.
    • Knowledge readiness – present knowledge base, cognitive ability and learning disabilities.
  • Implication – choose the right time, create a comfortable environment, reduce anxiety, link with previous knowledge.

3. Learning styles

  • Meaning – the preferred way in which a person takes in, processes and remembers information.
  • VARK model (Neil Fleming)
    • Visual – learn best from diagrams, charts, videos.
    • Aural – from lectures, discussions, audio.
    • Read/write – from notes, books, written assignments.
    • Kinaesthetic – from hands-on practice, demonstrations, simulation.
  • Kolb's learning styles – diverging (feel and watch), assimilating (think and watch), converging (think and do) and accommodating (feel and do).
  • Honey and Mumford – activists (learn by doing), reflectors (observe and think), theorists (logical models) and pragmatists (practical application).

Implications for the teacher

  • Use varied methods and media to suit different styles (multisensory teaching).
  • Begin with learners' needs and existing knowledge.
  • Time sessions when learners are alert; motivate them by showing relevance.
  • Give individual attention and remedial teaching to slow learners and challenges to fast learners.

Conclusion Learning depends on the learner's needs (the gap between present and desired competence), readiness (physical, emotional, experiential and knowledge – PEEK) and learning style (VARK, Kolb, Honey and Mumford). Assessing these helps the teacher plan content, methods and timing that make learning effective.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the characteristics of today's generation of learners and their implications for nursing education.
answer_html:
Introduction

  • Most students in nursing colleges today belong to Generation Z (born roughly between the mid-1990s and the early 2010s), followed by Generation Alpha; many teachers belong to earlier generations.
  • Understanding today's learners helps teachers adapt their methods.

Characteristics

  1. Digital natives – grew up with smartphones and the internet; comfortable with technology, social media and online resources.
  2. Prefer visual and interactive content – short videos, images, infographics, games rather than long lectures and textbooks.
  3. Short attention span and multitasking – easily distracted; switch rapidly between tasks.
  4. Want immediate feedback and quick results.
  5. Practical and goal-oriented – want to know the relevance of what they learn ("Why do I need this?").
  6. Collaborative – like group work and peer learning; also value individuality.
  7. Expect flexibility – anytime, anywhere access to learning materials.
  8. Information is easily available but they may have difficulty judging the reliability of sources (information overload).
  9. Socially aware – interested in social issues, diversity and fairness.
  10. Higher levels of stress and anxiety for many; may need more emotional support.
  11. Less reading of long texts; preference for summaries.

Implications for nursing education

  • Active and learner-centred methods – case discussions, PBL, team-based learning, simulation, role play, gaming.
  • Use of technology – learning management systems, e-content, videos, online quizzes, virtual simulation; blended and flipped classrooms.
  • Microlearning – short, focused segments (10–15 minutes) with frequent interaction.
  • Show relevance – link content to real patient situations and clinical practice.
  • Frequent, constructive feedback and formative assessment.
  • Teach information literacy – evaluating sources, evidence-based practice, avoiding plagiarism.
  • Digital professionalism – responsible use of social media, protecting patient confidentiality and privacy.
  • Mentoring and counselling – attention to well-being, stress and mental health.
  • Clear expectations and structure while allowing some flexibility.
  • Teachers' own updating in technology and new methods.

Teachers should also remember that "digital natives" are not automatically skilled in using technology for learning; they need guidance on deep reading, reflection and focused study without distraction.

Conclusion Today's learners are digital natives who prefer visual, interactive, relevant and flexible learning, expect quick feedback and work well in groups, but may have short attention spans and more stress. Nursing educators respond with active, technology-supported, relevant and supportive teaching while developing information literacy and digital professionalism.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the course plan and the unit plan.
answer_html:
Introduction Teaching is planned at three levels – the course plan (for the whole course or subject), the unit plan (for each unit of the course) and the lesson plan (for each session). Each is derived from the curriculum.

1. Course plan

  • Definition – a written plan of a complete course (subject) for a semester or year, prepared by the course teacher(s), showing what will be taught, when, how and how it will be evaluated.
  • Components
    • Course title, code, placement (year/semester), credits and theory, lab and clinical hours.
    • Course description – a brief statement of the scope of the course.
    • Course objectives/competencies (learning outcomes).
    • Units – titles, hours, learning outcomes, content outline.
    • Teaching–learning methods and activities for each unit (lecture, demonstration, seminar, skill lab, clinical).
    • Assessment plan – internal assessment (tests, assignments, practicals), weightage and the end-semester examination.
    • Schedule – timetable of classes and examinations.
    • References – textbooks and other resources.
  • Uses – ensures that the course is completed within the allotted time, provides continuity, helps coordination among teachers and informs students of expectations.

2. Unit plan

  • Definition – a plan for teaching one unit (a meaningful block of related content) of the course, usually covering several lessons.
  • Components
    • Unit title and number of hours.
    • Unit objectives (learning outcomes).
    • Content outline – topics and subtopics in sequence.
    • Time allotted to each topic.
    • Teaching–learning methods and activities for each topic.
    • AV aids and resources.
    • Assignments and student activities.
    • Evaluation – methods and tools for assessing achievement of unit objectives.
    • References.
  • Steps – analysing the unit content, writing objectives, dividing content into lessons, deciding methods and media, planning evaluation and assignments.
  • Advantages – gives a wider perspective than a lesson plan; ensures logical sequence and integration of topics; helps preparation of lesson plans; avoids gaps and repetition.

Relationship – curriculum → course plan → unit plans → lesson plans; each level becomes more specific.

Example (unit plan entry) – Unit: "Wound care", 6 hours; objective: "The student will perform a surgical dressing using aseptic technique"; methods: lecture-cum-discussion, demonstration, return demonstration in the skill lab; evaluation: checklist-based skill assessment.

Conclusion The course plan outlines an entire subject – description, objectives, units, hours, methods, assessment and schedule – while the unit plan details the objectives, content, time, methods, aids, assignments and evaluation of one unit; together with lesson plans they translate the curriculum into classroom practice.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: What are the types of learners?
answer_html:
Learners may be classified in different ways: 1. By learning style (VARK)

  • Visual – learn best by seeing (charts, diagrams, videos).
  • Auditory – learn by listening (lectures, discussions).
  • Read/write – learn through reading and writing notes.
  • Kinaesthetic – learn by doing (practice, demonstration, simulation). 2. By speed and ability – gifted/fast learners, average learners and slow learners. 3. By approach (Honey and Mumford) – activists, reflectors, theorists and pragmatists. 4. By age – children (pedagogy) and adult learners (andragogy – self-directed, experience-based and problem-centred). Knowing the types helps the teacher use varied methods and give individual attention.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: State the principles of preparing a course plan.
answer_html:
Principles of preparing a course plan

  1. Based on the curriculum – follow the regulatory body's (INC/university) syllabus, credits and hours.
  2. Clear course objectives (learning outcomes) in all domains.
  3. Logical sequence of units – simple to complex, with correlation to other courses and clinical postings.
  4. Realistic time allocation for theory, lab and clinical components, including time for revision and evaluation.
  5. Variety of teaching–learning methods suited to content and learners.
  6. Integration of theory and practice.
  7. Built-in evaluation plan – internal assessment and examinations.
  8. Flexibility to adjust for holidays and unforeseen events.
  9. Availability of resources – faculty, labs, clinical areas.
  10. Prepared jointly by the teachers concerned and communicated to students at the start.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: What is the hidden curriculum?
answer_html:
The hidden curriculum is the unplanned, unwritten and often unintended learning that students acquire from the culture, environment and behaviour of people in an institution, rather than from the formal syllabus.

  • It includes values, attitudes, norms and behaviours learnt by observing teachers, senior students and clinical staff – for example, how staff talk to patients, punctuality, respect for privacy, hierarchy, attitudes to night duty or to the poor.
  • It can be positive (caring, ethical role models) or negative (rudeness, shortcuts in procedures). Importance – it strongly shapes professional socialisation and identity; teachers must therefore be conscious role models and create a caring, ethical learning culture.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: (a) Explain the principles and strategies of classroom management. (8 marks) (b) Describe effective classroom communication, with its facilitators and barriers. (7 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Principles and strategies of classroom management (8 marks) Meaning

  • Classroom management is the set of actions a teacher takes to create and maintain an orderly, positive and productive learning environment in which teaching and learning can take place effectively.
  • It includes organising the physical setting, time, rules, activities and relationships, and handling problems of behaviour.

Principles of classroom management

  1. Preparation and planning – a well-prepared teacher with a clear lesson plan has fewer management problems.
  2. Clear expectations – rules and routines are explained at the beginning of the course (punctuality, attendance, mobile phone use, respect).
  3. Consistency and fairness – rules are applied equally to all; no favouritism.
  4. Positive learning climate – mutual respect, warmth and freedom to ask questions without fear.
  5. Active engagement – involving students keeps their attention and reduces disruption.
  6. Prevention rather than punishment – anticipate problems and prevent them.
  7. Positive reinforcement – praise and recognition of desirable behaviour.
  8. Respect for individual differences – varied needs, abilities and backgrounds.
  9. Effective communication – clear instructions, good listening, two-way interaction.
  10. Flexibility – adapting plans to the situation.
  11. Self-discipline – the teacher's own punctuality, dress and conduct set the example.

Strategies of classroom management 1. Managing the physical environment

  • Adequate space, lighting, ventilation and comfortable seating; reduction of noise.
  • Seating arrangement suited to the method – rows for lectures, U-shape or circle for discussion, clusters for group work.

  • AV aids and equipment checked before class; teacher positioned where all students can see and hear. 2. Establishing rules and routines

  • Discuss and agree on ground rules (time, phones on silent, raising hands, respectful disagreement).

  • Routines for attendance, distribution of material, submission of assignments. 3. Time management

  • Start and end on time; allocate time for introduction, development, activities and summary; avoid long monotonous talks. 4. Engaging students actively

  • Begin with an interesting introduction (case, question, video).

  • Use questioning, discussion, short group tasks, quizzes, think–pair–share and clinical examples.
  • Vary the pace, voice and methods; use AV aids.

  • Move around the class and make eye contact. 5. Motivation and reinforcement

  • Show relevance to patient care; set achievable challenges; give praise and constructive feedback; recognise effort. 6. Building relationships

  • Learn students' names; be approachable and empathetic; respect students' opinions; maintain professional boundaries. 7. Managing disruptive behaviour

  • Prevent by engagement and clear expectations.

  • Respond early and calmly – a look, moving closer, a pause, calling the student by name, asking a question.
  • Private discussion with the student after class rather than public humiliation; find the cause (fatigue, personal problems, lack of interest).

  • Logical consequences applied consistently; referral to the mentor or counsellor if needed; involve the class coordinator for persistent problems. 8. Managing large classes

  • Use a microphone and clear visuals; divide into groups; use student leaders; online quizzes and response tools; structured notes. 9. Managing technology – clear policy on mobile phones and laptops; use them purposefully for learning (online polls, e-resources). 10. Evaluation and feedback – check understanding during the class; obtain feedback from students about teaching.

Qualities of a well-managed class – students are punctual, attentive and involved; the atmosphere is friendly but purposeful; time is used well; problems are few and handled quietly.

(b) Effective classroom communication (7 marks) Meaning
