  • Classroom communication is the two-way exchange of ideas, information, feelings and instructions between the teacher and students, and among students, through verbal and non-verbal means.
  • Effective communication is the heart of teaching – learning happens only when the message is received and understood.

Elements – sender (teacher), message (content), channel (speech, writing, media), receiver (students), feedback, and the context and possible "noise".

Components of effective classroom communication

  1. Verbal communication
    • Clear, audible voice with suitable pitch, pace and variation.
    • Simple language; explanation of technical terms; examples and stories.
    • Logical organisation – introduction, main points, summary.
  2. Non-verbal communication
    • Eye contact, facial expression, gestures and posture.
    • Movement in the class; appropriate dress; enthusiasm.
  3. Questioning skills – questions at different levels (recall to reasoning), distributed to all students, with waiting time; encouraging students' questions.
  4. Active listening – attention to students' answers and questions; acknowledging contributions.
  5. Feedback – immediate, specific and constructive; praise for correct answers; gentle correction.
  6. Use of AV aids and technology – to support, not replace, communication.
  7. Written communication – clear handouts, board work and instructions.

Facilitators of classroom communication

  • Teacher factors – mastery of the subject, preparation, enthusiasm, clear speech, approachability, respect, sense of humour, good listening.
  • Student factors – interest, readiness, motivation, attention, previous knowledge, confidence to speak.
  • Environment – good acoustics, lighting, comfortable seating, small or well-managed groups, freedom from noise and interruptions.
  • Methods – interactive methods, questioning, discussion, use of examples and AV aids.
  • Climate – mutual trust, respect and freedom to express opinions.

Barriers to classroom communication

  1. Teacher-related
    • Poor preparation, unclear or too fast speech, low voice, monotony.
    • Excessive jargon; reading from slides.
    • Lack of eye contact; authoritarian or sarcastic attitude.
    • Ignoring students' questions; distracting mannerisms.
  2. Student-related
    • Lack of interest or attention; fatigue (after night duty); anxiety and fear of being ridiculed.
    • Shyness; poor language proficiency; preoccupation with personal problems; use of mobile phones.
  3. Physical/environmental
    • Noise, poor acoustics, overcrowding, poor lighting and ventilation.
    • Uncomfortable seating, faulty AV equipment, interruptions.
  4. Semantic (language) – difference in language or dialect, ambiguous words, technical terms without explanation.
  5. Psychological – prejudice, emotional barriers, negative relationships, low motivation.
  6. Organisational – very large classes, tight schedules, heavy content, lack of time for interaction.
  7. Cultural – differences in values and norms (e.g. students unwilling to question a teacher).

Overcoming barriers

  • Thorough preparation and clear objectives; simple language with explanations; varied voice and methods.
  • Encouraging questions and participation; creating a safe atmosphere; giving feedback.
  • Checking understanding (questions, teach-back, quizzes); using bilingual explanations where needed.
  • Improving the physical environment and checking equipment in advance; managing class size through groups.
  • Building good teacher–student relationships; addressing individual difficulties through mentoring.

Classroom management in clinical and skill-lab settings – the same principles apply outside the classroom: clear instructions before a demonstration, small groups at each station, a fixed sequence of practice, safety rules (sharps, infection control), time limits for each student and immediate feedback. In the ward, the teacher briefs students before the shift, assigns patients, supervises discreetly without embarrassing students in front of patients, and holds a post-clinical conference to discuss experiences.

Conclusion Classroom management creates an orderly, positive environment through principles of planning, clear expectations, consistency, engagement, reinforcement and prevention, and through strategies for the physical setting, rules, time, motivation, relationships, disruptive behaviour, large classes and technology. Effective classroom communication – clear verbal and non-verbal messages, questioning, listening and feedback – is helped by prepared, approachable teachers, motivated students and a good environment, and hindered by teacher, student, physical, language, psychological, organisational and cultural barriers that the teacher can overcome.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: (a) Define active learning and state its advantages. (3 marks) (b) Explain problem-based learning and team-based learning. (8 marks) (c) Describe other active learning strategies – peer sharing, case study analysis, journaling, debate, gaming and interprofessional education. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Problem-based learning and team-based learning
labels: team readiness test (tRAT) with immediate feedback

answer_html:
(a) Active learning and its advantages (3 marks) Definition

  • Active learning is any instructional method that engages students in doing meaningful learning activities and thinking about what they are doing, rather than passively listening.
  • Students read, write, discuss, solve problems, practise skills, reflect and teach each other; the teacher acts as a facilitator.

Advantages

  • Promotes deep understanding and better retention than passive lectures.
  • Develops critical thinking, problem-solving, clinical reasoning and decision-making.
  • Improves communication, teamwork and leadership skills.
  • Increases motivation, interest and attendance; suits today's learners.
  • Encourages self-directed and lifelong learning.
  • Gives teachers immediate information about students' understanding.

(b) Problem-based learning and team-based learning (8 marks) 1. Problem-based learning (PBL)

  • Definition – a learner-centred approach in which students learn by working in small groups on real-life problems (scenarios); the problem comes first and drives the learning.
  • Origin – developed by Howard Barrows and colleagues at McMaster University, Canada (late 1960s) for medical education; now widely used in nursing.
  • Features
    • Small groups (6–10 students) with a tutor/facilitator.
    • Ill-structured, realistic problems that need knowledge from several subjects.
    • Self-directed learning between sessions.
    • Emphasis on reasoning, collaboration and reflection.
  • Steps (based on the "seven-jump" approach)
    1. Read the problem and clarify unfamiliar terms.
    2. Define the problem(s).
    3. Brainstorm possible explanations using prior knowledge.
    4. Organise ideas and develop hypotheses.
    5. Formulate learning issues (objectives).
    6. Self-directed study using books, journals and other resources.
    7. Report back and synthesise new knowledge in the group; apply to the problem; reflect on the process.
  • Example – "A 55-year-old farmer with diabetes has a non-healing foot ulcer and says he cannot afford regular dressings." Learning issues: pathophysiology of diabetic foot, wound care, nutrition, health schemes, patient education.
  • Role of the tutor – guides the process with questions, keeps the group on track, encourages participation and evaluates; does not lecture.
  • Advantages – integrates basic and clinical knowledge, develops reasoning, self-directed learning and teamwork, increases motivation.
  • Limitations – time-consuming; needs many trained tutors, resources and library access; students may feel insecure about "what to learn"; may cover less content.

2. Team-based learning (TBL)

  • Definition – a structured form of small-group learning, developed by Larry Michaelsen (1970s), in which permanent teams (5–7 students) apply course concepts to problems, with individual and team accountability; it can be used in large classes with one teacher.
  • Phases
    1. Pre-class preparation – students study assigned materials (readings, videos) individually.
    2. Readiness assurance process (RAP) in class
      • Individual readiness assurance test (iRAT) – short MCQ test answered individually.
      • Team readiness assurance test (tRAT) – the same test answered by the team through discussion, often with immediate-feedback (scratch) cards.
      • Appeals – teams may challenge answers with evidence.
      • Mini-lecture – the teacher clarifies concepts that were difficult.
    3. Application exercises – teams solve complex clinical problems using the "4 S" principles:
      • Significant problem relevant to practice;
      • Same problem for all teams;
      • Specific choice – teams must make a decision;
      • Simultaneous reporting – all teams reveal their answers together, followed by discussion between teams.
    4. Peer evaluation – team members assess each other's contribution.
  • Advantages – ensures preparation and accountability; develops application, reasoning and teamwork; efficient for large classes; immediate feedback.
  • Limitations – requires careful preparation of tests and exercises; students must be willing to prepare beforehand; may cause conflicts in teams.

Difference in brief – PBL starts with a problem and students identify what to learn, with a tutor for each small group; TBL starts with prepared content, tests readiness and then applies it, with one teacher managing many teams.

(c) Other active learning strategies (4 marks)

  1. Peer sharing (peer learning) – students teach and learn from each other; e.g. think–pair–share (think individually, discuss with a partner, share with the class), peer demonstration, peer tutoring and study groups. Builds confidence and communication.
  2. Case study analysis – students analyse a detailed case of a real or simulated patient, identify problems, plan care and justify decisions; promotes application of theory and clinical reasoning.
  3. Journaling – students write reflective journals about clinical and learning experiences, their feelings and lessons learnt; develops reflection, self-awareness and writing skills (Gibbs' reflective cycle).
  4. Debate – two teams argue for and against an issue (e.g. "Euthanasia should be legalised", "Nurses should prescribe medicines"); develops research, reasoning, communication and respect for other views.
  5. Gaming and gamification – educational games such as quizzes, crosswords, board games, "escape rooms", online games and points/leaderboards; makes learning enjoyable and reinforces knowledge.
  6. Interprofessional education (IPE) – students of nursing, medicine, pharmacy and allied health learn with, from and about each other (e.g. joint simulation of a cardiac arrest or ward round); improves teamwork, communication and patient safety.

Role of the teacher in active learning – plans activities linked to outcomes, prepares materials, explains the process, facilitates rather than dominates, manages time and groups, gives feedback and evaluates both process and outcomes.

Simple active learning techniques that can be used even in a lecture

  • One-minute paper – at the end of the class, students write the most important point learnt and one question that remains.
  • Muddiest point – students write what was least clear, so the teacher can clarify in the next class.
  • Concept checks and quick polls – an MCQ is projected and students answer by raising cards or using an online poll; answers are discussed.
  • Buzz groups – small groups discuss a question for a few minutes and report back.
  • Jigsaw – each member of a group studies one part of a topic, and then teaches it to the others.
  • Case-based questions – a short patient scenario is presented and students decide the priority action.

Assessment in active learning – active learning is assessed through participation records, peer evaluation, readiness tests, case presentations, reflective journals, rubrics for group products and application-level examination questions, rather than only recall.

Challenges and how to overcome them

  • Students may initially resist because they are used to passive learning – explain the purpose and benefits, start with short simple activities.
  • Covering the syllabus may seem difficult – combine pre-class reading or videos with in-class application (flipped classroom).
  • Large classes and limited space – use pair and small-group activities, student leaders and online tools.
  • Teachers need training – faculty development workshops and sharing of experiences.

Conclusion Active learning engages students in doing and thinking, improving understanding, reasoning, teamwork and motivation. Problem-based learning (Barrows) uses real problems in small tutored groups with self-directed study, while team-based learning (Michaelsen) uses preparation, readiness tests and application exercises in permanent teams. Peer sharing, case study analysis, journaling, debate, gaming and interprofessional education add variety and develop critical thinking and collaboration.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain microteaching – its meaning, steps (cycle) and teaching skills.
answer_html:
Meaning Microteaching is a scaled-down teaching encounter used to train teachers in specific teaching skills. It was developed at Stanford University (USA) in 1963 by Dwight W. Allen and colleagues. It is "micro" because the class size (5–10 students), duration (5–10 minutes), content (a small concept) and skill (one at a time) are reduced.

Microteaching cycle (steps)

  1. Plan – the trainee selects one skill and a small topic and prepares a micro-lesson plan.
  2. Teach – teaches the micro-lesson to a small group while a supervisor or peers observe (often video-recorded).
  3. Feedback – the supervisor and peers give feedback on the use of the skill, using an observation schedule.
  4. Replan – the trainee revises the lesson in the light of feedback.
  5. Reteach – teaches the revised lesson to another small group.
  6. Re-feedback – further feedback; the cycle continues until mastery.

Indian model (time schedule) – teach 6 minutes, feedback 6 minutes, replan 12 minutes, reteach 6 minutes, re-feedback 6 minutes – a total of 36 minutes.

Important teaching skills practised

  1. Skill of set induction (introducing a lesson) – arousing interest and linking with previous knowledge (a question, case, picture).
  2. Skill of explaining – clear, logical explanation with examples and connecting links.
  3. Skill of questioning – fluency in asking questions, probing questions, distribution and pausing.
  4. Skill of reinforcement – positive verbal (praise) and non-verbal (smile, nod) reinforcement; avoiding negative reinforcement.
  5. Skill of stimulus variation – changes in movement, gestures, voice, focusing, interaction styles and media to maintain attention.
  6. Skill of illustrating with examples – simple, relevant, interesting examples.
  7. Skill of using the blackboard/whiteboard – legible, well-organised writing and diagrams.
  8. Skill of closure – summarising and linking to future learning.
  9. Others – skill of demonstration, use of AV aids, classroom management.

Advantages

  • Focuses on one skill at a time; reduces complexity of real teaching.
  • Immediate, objective feedback, often supported by video recording.
  • Safe practice environment; builds confidence of new teachers.
  • Helps both pre-service and in-service teacher training; useful for nursing faculty development and student-teaching practice.

Limitations

  • Artificial situation; small groups do not reflect real classes.
  • Time-consuming; needs trained supervisors and facilities.
  • Integration of skills into a full lesson needs further practice ("link practice").

Conclusion Microteaching, developed at Stanford in 1963, is a scaled-down teaching–feedback cycle (plan, teach, feedback, replan, reteach, re-feedback – 36 minutes in the Indian model) used to master specific skills such as set induction, explaining, questioning, reinforcement, stimulus variation, illustration, board work and closure.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the lecture method – its preparation, merits and demerits, and ways to make it effective.
answer_html:
Definition The lecture method is a teacher-centred method in which the teacher presents information orally to a group of learners, usually with the help of AV aids, in a planned and organised way. It is the oldest and most widely used method.

Types – formal lecture, lecture-cum-discussion, lecture-cum-demonstration and interactive lecture (with questions, quizzes and short activities).

Preparation

  1. Define the objectives and know the learners' previous knowledge.
  2. Collect and select relevant, up-to-date content; organise it logically.
  3. Prepare a lesson plan with time for each part.
  4. Prepare AV aids (slides, charts, models, video clips) and handouts.
  5. Rehearse; check the room and equipment in advance.

Delivery – three parts

  • Introduction (5–10%) – arouse interest (a case, question, story, statistic), state objectives, link with previous knowledge.
  • Body (80%) – present main points in logical sequence (simple to complex), with explanations, examples and visuals; check understanding through questions; vary voice and pace.
  • Conclusion (10%) – summarise key points, answer questions, give assignments and references.

Merits

  • Economical – one teacher can teach a large group.
  • Covers a large amount of content in a short time.
  • Gives an overview and organises scattered information; introduces new topics.
  • The teacher can share recent advances and personal experiences.
  • Inspires students through an enthusiastic speaker.
  • Suitable for imparting factual knowledge and when resources are limited.

Demerits

  • Teacher-centred and one-way; students are passive.
  • Attention declines after about 15–20 minutes; much content is forgotten.
  • Does not suit individual differences or develop skills and attitudes.
  • Little opportunity for critical thinking and feedback.
  • Effectiveness depends heavily on the teacher's ability.

Making lectures effective

  • Limit content to a few key points; follow the maxims of teaching.
  • Break the lecture into 15–20-minute segments with activities – questions, think–pair–share, short quizzes, case examples.
  • Use AV aids (but avoid reading slides); give handouts.
  • Maintain eye contact, a clear voice, enthusiasm and movement.
  • Relate content to clinical practice; use stories and examples.
  • Encourage questions; summarise frequently.
  • Combine with other methods – discussion, demonstration, flipped classroom.

Conclusion The lecture is an economical, efficient method for presenting organised information to large groups, but it is one-way and passive; careful preparation, a clear introduction–body–conclusion structure, AV aids, interaction and short segments make it effective.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the symposium as a method of teaching.
tags: difference from panel discussion and seminar
answer_html:
Definition A symposium is a group presentation in which two to five experts or well-prepared speakers present short, formal speeches on different aspects of a single topic, one after another, under the direction of a chairperson (moderator), followed by questions and discussion from the audience.

Purposes

  • To present different aspects or viewpoints of a topic in a short time.
  • To give the audience in-depth, authoritative information from different specialists.
  • To stimulate thinking and discussion.
  • To develop presentation, research and organisational skills among students.

Organisation 1. Planning

  • Select a topic of interest with several aspects – e.g. "Prevention of hospital-acquired infections": (i) epidemiology and types, (ii) hand hygiene and standard precautions, (iii) biomedical waste management, (iv) role of the infection control nurse.
  • Select the chairperson and speakers; assign aspects; fix time (usually 10–15 minutes per speaker, total about 60–90 minutes).

  • Inform the audience in advance; arrange the hall, seating, microphone and AV aids. 2. Conduct

  • The chairperson introduces the topic, the purpose and the speakers, controls the time, links the presentations and conducts the question session.

  • Each speaker presents his or her aspect formally, using AV aids, without interruption.
  • After all presentations, the audience asks questions; speakers answer; open discussion follows.
  • The chairperson summarises the main points and concludes. 3. Evaluation – feedback from the audience and teacher on content, presentation and organisation.

Physical arrangement – speakers and chairperson seated on a platform facing the audience; the chairperson in the centre.

Advantages

  • Several aspects of a topic covered by experts in a short time.
  • Formal and well-organised; suitable for large groups.
  • Students learn public speaking, research and presentation skills.
  • Stimulates interest and further reading.

Limitations

  • Little interaction between speakers; the audience is mostly passive until the question time.
  • Speakers may overlap or exceed their time.
  • Requires careful planning and competent speakers and chairperson.

Difference from panel discussion – in a symposium, speakers give prepared, formal speeches on separate aspects; in a panel discussion, panel members hold an informal conversation among themselves on the topic in front of the audience.

Role of the teacher – selects topics, guides students in preparation, acts as or trains the chairperson, ensures timing and evaluates.

Conclusion A symposium is a formal series of short speeches by two to five speakers on different aspects of one topic under a chairperson, followed by audience questions; it gives comprehensive information and develops presentation skills, but offers limited interaction and needs careful organisation.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the seminar as a method of teaching.
answer_html:
Definition A seminar is a group learning method in which one or more students (or participants) present a paper on a topic after detailed study, followed by critical discussion among all participants under the guidance of a seminar leader (teacher/moderator). It is an important method in higher education.

Purposes

  • To develop self-study, library and research skills.
  • To promote critical thinking, analysis and logical reasoning.
  • To improve presentation and communication skills.
  • To encourage participation and exchange of ideas.
  • To develop leadership and the ability to accept criticism.

Types – mini-seminar (within a class), major seminar (larger group), clinical seminar (on a patient or clinical problem), journal club–type seminar, and international or national seminars (conferences).

Organisation (steps)

  1. Planning – the teacher selects topics according to objectives and assigns them to students well in advance (2–3 weeks); provides references and guidelines.
  2. Preparation by the presenter – studies the topic from books, journals and internet sources; prepares a written paper and AV aids; discusses the draft with the guide.
  3. Arrangement – circular or U-shaped seating; AV equipment; copies of the paper or summary circulated to participants in advance so they can prepare questions.
  4. Presentation – the chairperson introduces the topic and presenter; the presenter presents for about 20–30 minutes.
  5. Discussion – participants ask questions, raise issues and give comments; the presenter clarifies; the leader guides the discussion and adds missing points.
  6. Summary – the chairperson or teacher summarises and concludes.
  7. Evaluation – based on criteria such as content and depth, organisation, use of references, presentation skills, use of AV aids, time management, ability to answer questions and participation of the group.

Roles

  • Teacher/seminar leader – guides, facilitates and evaluates.
  • Presenter – prepares and presents the paper.
  • Chairperson – introduces, controls time and conducts discussion (can be a student).
  • Participants – read in advance, listen, question and discuss.

Advantages – active learning; develops research, presentation, critical thinking and leadership; promotes in-depth understanding and confidence; students learn to accept and give constructive criticism.

Limitations – time-consuming; suitable only for small groups and senior students; quality depends on the presenter; others may not prepare; some may dominate the discussion.

Conclusion A seminar is a group method in which a student presents a carefully prepared paper followed by critical discussion under a leader; it develops self-study, research, critical thinking and presentation skills, though it needs time, preparation and active participation by all.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the workshop as a method of teaching and learning.
answer_html:
Definition A workshop is an intensive, practical, participatory learning programme in which a group of people with common interests work together under expert guidance to acquire skills or solve a specific problem, usually over one or more days. The emphasis is on learning by doing and producing an outcome.

Purposes

  • To develop practical skills (e.g. neonatal resuscitation, writing objectives, constructing MCQs).
  • To solve problems or prepare materials (e.g. preparing a curriculum, a nursing procedure manual).
  • To update knowledge and exchange experiences.
  • To promote teamwork and professional development (continuing nursing education).

Characteristics – a specific theme; small groups; experts as resource persons; a mix of brief presentations and hands-on group work; participants produce something concrete (a plan, a tool, a skill); evaluation at the end.

Phases

  1. Planning phase
    • Identify the need and objectives; select the theme, resource persons and participants (usually 15–30).
    • Fix dates, venue and budget; prepare the schedule, materials and equipment; send invitations and pre-reading.
  2. Introductory (orientation) session
    • Inauguration, introduction of participants and resource persons, objectives and schedule; pre-test.
  3. Working sessions
    • Short lectures or demonstrations by experts.
    • Group work – participants divided into small groups for practice, exercises, case discussions and preparation of products under guidance.
    • Hands-on practice on models or simulators.
  4. Plenary (reporting) session
    • Groups present their work; discussion and feedback; consolidation of outcomes.
  5. Evaluation and follow-up
    • Post-test, feedback on the workshop, certificates; report preparation; follow-up of implementation.

Examples in nursing – workshops on basic life support, infection control, preparation of lesson plans and question papers, research methodology, OSCE station design, breastfeeding counselling.

Advantages

  • Active participation, learning by doing, practical skills.
  • Immediate application; tangible outputs.
  • Exchange of ideas and experiences among participants; networking.
  • Motivation and professional development.

Limitations

  • Needs careful planning, time, resources and expert facilitators; expensive.
  • Suitable for small groups only.
  • Participants must be motivated and have basic knowledge; follow-up is often lacking.

Conclusion A workshop is an intensive, participatory programme in which participants work in groups under experts to develop skills or solve problems, passing through planning, introduction, working sessions, plenary and evaluation phases; it gives practical, applied learning but needs planning and resources.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain role play as a teaching method.
answer_html:
Definition Role play is a teaching method in which learners act out a real-life situation by taking the roles of people involved (e.g. nurse, patient, relative, doctor) in a spontaneous way, followed by discussion of feelings, behaviour and lessons learnt. It is especially useful for the affective domain and communication skills.

Purposes

  • To develop communication, interpersonal and counselling skills.
  • To understand feelings and viewpoints of others (empathy).
  • To practise handling difficult situations safely (breaking bad news, an angry relative, refusing medication).
  • To explore attitudes, values and ethical dilemmas.
  • To apply theory to practice.

Types – structured (scripted roles and dialogue), unstructured (spontaneous), role reversal (e.g. the student nurse plays the patient), and simulated patient role play.

Steps

  1. Preparation – select a situation linked to objectives; write a brief scenario and role descriptions; decide the time (10–15 minutes).
  2. Selection of players and observers – volunteers take roles; others are observers with observation guidelines.
  3. Briefing (warming up) – explain the situation, roles and purpose; create a non-threatening atmosphere.
  4. Enactment – participants act out the roles; the teacher does not interrupt unless necessary.
  5. Debriefing and discussion – players first express how they felt; observers comment on what went well and what could be improved; the group discusses alternatives and principles.
  6. Re-enactment (optional) – trying a better approach.
  7. Summary and evaluation – the teacher summarises the learning points.

Examples in nursing

  • Admission of an anxious patient; obtaining informed consent.
  • Health teaching of a diabetic patient; counselling for family planning or HIV testing.
  • Communicating with a hearing-impaired client; handling a complaint.
  • Breaking bad news to a family; handover between shifts.

Advantages

  • Active, interesting and enjoyable; develops empathy and communication.
  • Safe practice of difficult situations; immediate feedback.
  • Helps understand attitudes and change behaviour.
  • Develops confidence and spontaneity.

Limitations

  • Some students feel shy or embarrassed; may not take it seriously.
  • May turn into entertainment without proper debriefing.
  • Time-consuming; needs a skilled facilitator; may arouse strong emotions.
  • Not suitable for teaching large amounts of content.

Conclusion Role play lets learners act out real-life situations to develop communication, empathy and problem-solving, through preparation, briefing, enactment, debriefing and evaluation; it is valuable for affective learning in nursing when guided by a skilled teacher.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain self-directed learning in nursing education.
answer_html:
Definition Self-directed learning (SDL) is a process in which individuals take the initiative, with or without help from others, in diagnosing their learning needs, formulating goals, identifying resources, choosing and implementing learning strategies and evaluating outcomes (Malcolm Knowles, 1975).

Basis – principles of adult learning (andragogy, Knowles)

  • Adults are self-directed, bring experience to learning, are ready to learn what is relevant to their roles, are problem-centred, and are motivated more by internal factors.

Characteristics of self-directed learners – curiosity, motivation, responsibility for one's own learning, time management, ability to find and evaluate information, self-discipline, reflection and self-evaluation.

Steps of self-directed learning

  1. Diagnosing learning needs – self-assessment, feedback from teachers, comparing with competencies.
  2. Formulating learning goals – specific and realistic.
  3. Identifying resources – books, journals, e-learning modules, videos, skill lab, clinical experts, peers.
  4. Choosing and implementing strategies – reading, practice, projects, online courses, discussion.
  5. Evaluating learning – self-tests, demonstration, portfolio, feedback. A learning contract – a written agreement between the student and teacher stating objectives, resources, strategies, evidence of accomplishment, criteria and time frame – helps structure SDL.

SDL in the INC curriculum – the B.Sc Nursing curriculum allots time for self-directed learning in many courses, in which students study assigned topics, prepare presentations or e-modules and practise skills independently.

Role of the teacher

  • Acts as a facilitator, resource person and mentor.
  • Helps students identify needs and set goals; provides access to resources (library, digital resources, skill lab).
  • Gives structure (guidelines, deadlines, learning contracts) and gradually increases independence.
  • Monitors progress, gives feedback and evaluates.

Advantages

  • Develops independence, responsibility and lifelong learning skills – essential in a profession where knowledge changes rapidly.
  • Learning at one's own pace and according to one's own style.
  • Promotes critical thinking, information literacy and confidence.

Challenges

  • Students used to teacher-centred learning may feel lost; poor time management; unequal access to resources; need for monitoring to prevent superficial learning.

Conclusion Self-directed learning, based on Knowles' andragogy, makes learners responsible for diagnosing needs, setting goals, finding resources, learning and evaluating outcomes, often through learning contracts; with the teacher as facilitator, it develops the independence and lifelong learning that nurses need.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the use of information and communication technology (ICT) in nursing education.
answer_html:
Meaning Information and communication technology (ICT) in education refers to the use of computers, the internet, digital devices, software and communication networks to create, store, share and deliver educational content and to support teaching, learning, assessment and administration.

ICT tools used in nursing education

  1. Learning management systems (LMS) – e.g. Moodle, Google Classroom – for posting notes, videos and assignments, online quizzes, discussion forums and tracking progress.
  2. E-content and open educational resources – e-books, recorded lectures, animations, procedure videos, e-modules.
  3. Online courses (MOOCs) – national platforms such as SWAYAM, and other online courses for continuing education.
  4. Virtual classrooms and video conferencing – live online lectures, guest lectures by experts from other places, tele-education.
  5. Smart classrooms – interactive smart boards, multimedia projectors, document cameras, classroom response systems (online polls, clickers).
  6. Digital libraries and databases – e-journals and databases (e.g. PubMed), institutional digital libraries for evidence-based learning.
  7. Simulation software and virtual reality – virtual patients, screen-based simulators, VR for anatomy and procedures.
  8. Mobile learning – apps for drug information, anatomy, clinical calculators, flashcards and quizzes.
  9. Online assessment tools – computer-based tests, e-portfolios, plagiarism-detection software.
  10. Communication tools – email, messaging groups and forums for mentoring and coordination.

Advantages

  • Access to up-to-date, varied resources anytime and anywhere.
  • Supports blended, flipped and distance learning.
  • Makes learning interactive, visual and self-paced; suits today's learners.
  • Enables simulation and repeated practice without risk to patients.
  • Efficient administration – attendance, records, results.
  • Facilitates collaboration and continuing professional development.

Challenges

  • Digital divide – lack of devices, internet connectivity and electricity in some areas.
  • Lack of training and confidence among teachers; resistance to change.
  • Cost of infrastructure and maintenance; technical problems.
  • Distraction, information overload and unreliable online information; plagiarism.
  • Reduced face-to-face interaction; risk to privacy and data security.

Role of the nurse teacher

  • Develop digital skills and integrate ICT purposefully into lesson plans.
  • Create and curate quality e-content; guide students to reliable sources.
  • Teach digital professionalism and ethics (confidentiality on social media, copyright, avoiding plagiarism).
  • Ensure equal access and blend ICT with practical and clinical teaching.

Conclusion ICT in nursing education includes LMS, e-content, MOOCs such as SWAYAM, virtual and smart classrooms, digital libraries, simulation and VR, mobile learning and online assessment; it makes learning accessible, interactive and flexible, but requires infrastructure, trained teachers and attention to the digital divide and ethics.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: List the barriers to classroom communication.
answer_html:
Barriers to classroom communication

  1. Teacher-related – poor preparation, unclear, fast or low speech, monotony, excessive jargon, reading from slides, lack of eye contact, sarcastic or authoritarian attitude, ignoring questions.
  2. Student-related – lack of interest or attention, fatigue, anxiety, shyness, poor language skills, use of mobile phones, personal problems.
  3. Physical/environmental – noise, poor acoustics, overcrowding, poor lighting and ventilation, faulty AV equipment, interruptions.
  4. Semantic (language) – differences in language, ambiguous words, unexplained technical terms.
  5. Psychological – prejudice, fear, poor teacher–student relationship.
  6. Organisational – large classes, heavy content, lack of time for interaction.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: What is a panel discussion?
answer_html:
A panel discussion is a group method in which a small group of 3–6 experts or well-informed persons (the panel) hold an informal, conversational discussion on a topic in front of an audience, under the guidance of a moderator.

  • The moderator introduces the topic and panel members, asks questions, keeps the discussion balanced and on time, and later invites questions from the audience; finally summarises.
  • Panel members do not give formal speeches (unlike a symposium); they exchange views spontaneously. Advantages – presents different viewpoints; lively and interesting; encourages critical thinking; suitable for controversial topics (e.g. "organ donation"). Limitations – may drift from the topic; some members may dominate; needs a skilled moderator.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: What is a field trip? State its value in nursing education.
answer_html:
A field trip (educational visit) is a planned visit by students to a place outside the classroom to observe and learn things in their natural setting.

  • Steps – planning (objectives, permission, schedule, guidelines), conduct (observation, guided explanation, note-taking) and follow-up (discussion, report writing, evaluation).
  • Examples – visits to a water purification plant, sewage treatment plant, milk dairy, PHC, District TB Centre, rehabilitation centre, old-age home, Anganwadi. Value – provides first-hand, real experience; links theory with practice; arouses interest and curiosity; develops observation and reporting skills; helps students understand health services and the community.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: What is the project method?
answer_html: The project method is a learner-centred method in which students learn by carrying out a purposeful, real-life task (project) from start to finish, individually or in groups. It was developed by W. H. Kilpatrick on the basis of John Dewey's pragmatism. Steps – (1) creating the situation, (2) choosing and purposing the project, (3) planning, (4) executing, (5) evaluating (judging) and (6) recording/reporting. Examples in nursing – preparing a health education exhibition, conducting a small community survey on anaemia, developing an information booklet for diabetic patients. Advantages – learning by doing, problem-solving, teamwork, responsibility and creativity; links learning with life.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: What is a skill laboratory? State its uses.
answer_html:
A skill laboratory (skill lab) is a specially equipped room or area where students learn and practise nursing procedures on models, manikins, task trainers and simulators, and with each other, under supervision, before performing them on patients.

  • It contains equipment and set-ups similar to the ward – beds, procedure trolleys, IV arms, injection pads, catheterisation and delivery models, CPR manikins and simulators. Uses

  • Demonstration and return demonstration of procedures; repeated practice until competence.

  • Safe practice without risk to patients; builds confidence.
  • Simulation-based learning and assessment (OSCE).
  • Practice of rare and emergency procedures. The INC curriculum includes mandatory skill-lab hours for many courses.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: (a) Explain the clinical learning environment and the factors influencing the selection of clinical learning experiences. (6 marks) (b) Describe the clinical teaching strategies. (9 marks)
tags: characteristics of good clinical learning environment
factors influencing selection of clinical learning experiences

diagram.caption: Components of the clinical learning environment
labels: ward nurses and the health team

answer_html:
(a) Clinical learning environment and selection of experiences (6 marks) Meaning

  • The clinical learning environment (CLE) is the interactive network of forces within the clinical setting – hospital wards, OPDs, operation theatres, community areas and homes – that influences students' clinical learning outcomes.
  • It is where students apply theory to real patients, develop skills, clinical judgement and professional values, and learn to work in a team. A large part of nursing education (more than half the hours) takes place here.

Components of the clinical learning environment

  1. Physical environment – the ward, equipment, supplies, space, case mix and patient load.
  2. Human environment – patients and families, clinical teachers, ward sisters and staff nurses, doctors and other health professionals, peers.
  3. Psychosocial environment (ward atmosphere) – acceptance and support of students, respect, teamwork, communication, freedom to ask questions, absence of humiliation.
  4. Organisational environment – hospital policies, nursing care delivery model, staffing, workload, ward routines, quality standards.
  5. Educational environment – clear learning outcomes, supervision, teaching activities, feedback, evaluation and coordination between college and hospital.

Characteristics of a good clinical learning environment

  • Students are welcomed and treated as learners and team members.
  • Adequate and varied patients relevant to the learning outcomes.
  • Availability of equipment and resources; good standards of care to observe (positive role models).
  • Supportive supervision by teachers and ward staff; constructive feedback.
  • Good communication and collaboration between the college and the hospital.
  • Emphasis on patient safety and ethical practice.
  • Opportunities for reflection and discussion (clinical conferences).

Factors influencing the selection of clinical learning experiences

  1. Learning outcomes/objectives of the course and clinical posting.
  2. Level of the students – year, previous knowledge, skills already learnt; progression from simple to complex.
  3. Availability and variety of patients – case mix, patient condition and acuity, willingness and consent of patients.
  4. Patient safety and welfare – assignments must not compromise care; patients' rights and dignity.
  5. Clinical facilities – type of hospital or community area, equipment and supplies.
  6. Qualified clinical teachers and staff available for supervision; teacher–student ratio.
  7. Time – duration of the posting, shift timings, number of students in the area.
  8. Learners' individual needs and interests – remedial or advanced experiences.
  9. Ward policies and routines – visiting hours, rounds, procedures allowed for students.
  10. Integration with classroom teaching – experiences should match topics taught.
  11. Opportunities for continuity of care – following a patient from admission to discharge.
  12. Evaluation requirements – logbook procedures and competencies to be completed.

(b) Clinical teaching strategies (9 marks)

  1. Patient (clinical) assignment
    • The teacher assigns one or more patients to each student for total care during the shift, according to objectives and level.
    • Methods – case method (total care), functional method, team assignment, primary nursing.
    • Develops responsibility, planning and organisation of care.
  2. Clinical conference
    • Pre-clinical conference before the shift to plan care.
    • Post-clinical conference after the shift to discuss experiences, problems and learning.
    • Other types – nursing care conference and topic conference.
  3. Bedside clinic
    • Teaching conducted at the patient's bedside in a small group – the student or teacher presents the patient, the group examines (with consent), discusses findings, nursing problems and care.
  4. Case study and care study
    • Case study – an in-depth study of a patient's disease, condition and management.
    • Care study – detailed nursing care given by the student to a patient over a period, with a written report: history, assessment, diagnoses, nursing care plan, implementation, evaluation and health education.
  5. Nursing rounds
    • Planned visits by a group of students with the teacher to several patients to observe and discuss their conditions and nursing care; types – teaching rounds, grand rounds, nursing care rounds.
  6. Concept mapping
    • A diagram linking the patient's problems, assessment data, nursing diagnoses, interventions and outcomes; develops critical thinking and holistic care.
  7. Demonstration and return demonstration – of procedures at the bedside or in the ward treatment room, followed by supervised practice.
  8. Questioning – Socratic and higher-order questions during care ("Why is this patient breathless?", "What will you do if the BP falls?") to develop reasoning.
  9. Written assignments
    • Nursing care plans, drug studies, health education plans, clinical logbooks, reflective journals and incident reports.
  10. Process recording – a verbatim record of nurse–patient interaction (especially in psychiatric nursing), analysed for communication techniques.
  11. Clinical presentation / case presentation – the student presents a patient to the group.
  12. Project – e.g. preparing a ward teaching chart, conducting a mini-audit of hand hygiene.
  13. Debate, games and role play – on clinical issues (e.g. restraint use), quizzes on drugs, role play of counselling or handover.
  14. Problem-based learning (PBL) – using real patients' problems for group learning.
  15. Simulation – before or alongside clinical practice for emergencies and rare situations.
  16. Preceptorship and mentorship – a staff nurse (preceptor) guides an individual student one-to-one during practice.
  17. Reflective journals and critical incident analysis – reflecting on experiences, feelings and lessons learnt.
  18. Health education sessions – students give health talks to patients and relatives in the ward or OPD.

Principles for effective clinical teaching

  • Clear objectives communicated to students and ward staff.
  • Planned rotation and assignments; orientation to each area.
  • Supervision proportional to the student's competence; patient safety first.
  • Immediate, private and constructive feedback.
  • Integration of theory with practice; encouraging reflection.
  • Regular evaluation with checklists, rating scales and logbooks.

Problems commonly faced in the clinical learning environment and remedies

  • Theory–practice gap – what is taught in class is not always practised in the ward; remedy: joint planning with ward staff, evidence-based protocols, demonstrations in the actual setting.
  • Students treated as extra hands for routine work; remedy: clear learning objectives shared with the ward in-charge and planned assignments.
  • Overcrowding of students in a ward and too few suitable patients; remedy: planned rotation, smaller groups, use of community and OPD areas, simulation.
  • Anxiety and fear of making mistakes; remedy: orientation, close supervision initially, supportive feedback and a culture of learning from errors.
  • Inadequate supervision due to a shortage of teachers; remedy: preceptorship and involvement of trained staff nurses.

Role of the college–hospital partnership – a formal agreement on student placement, orientation of ward staff to the curriculum, shared responsibility for supervision and evaluation, regular meetings, and recognition of staff who teach students strengthen the clinical learning environment.

Students' responsibilities in the clinical area – punctuality, correct uniform and identity card, preparation before the shift, safe practice within limits, reporting to the teacher and in-charge, maintaining confidentiality, accurate documentation and completing logbooks.

Conclusion The clinical learning environment – physical, human, psychosocial, organisational and educational – shapes how students learn to care for real patients; clinical experiences are selected according to objectives, student level, patient availability and safety, facilities, teachers, time and policies. Clinical teaching uses strategies such as patient assignment, clinical conferences, bedside clinics, case and care studies, nursing rounds, concept mapping, demonstration, questioning, written assignments, process recording, presentations, projects, debate, games, role play, PBL, simulation, preceptorship and reflective journals.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain concept mapping as a clinical teaching strategy.
tags: steps of preparing a care concept map
answer_html:
Definition

  • A concept map is a diagram that shows relationships between concepts using boxes (nodes) connected by labelled lines or arrows.
  • It was developed by Joseph Novak (1970s) on the basis of Ausubel's theory of meaningful learning – new knowledge is linked with what the learner already knows.
  • In clinical teaching, a care map (nursing concept map) shows how a patient's medical diagnosis, assessment data, nursing diagnoses, interventions and expected outcomes are interrelated.

Components

  • Concepts – key ideas in boxes or ovals (e.g. "dehydration", "low BP").
  • Linking words on the lines (e.g. "causes", "leads to", "requires").
  • Propositions – two concepts joined by linking words forming a meaningful statement.
  • Hierarchy – general concepts at the top or centre, specific ones around them.
  • Cross-links – connections between different areas of the map.

Steps in preparing a patient care concept map

  1. Place the patient's main problem or medical diagnosis in the centre (e.g. "Congestive cardiac failure").
  2. Around it, write the assessment data – signs, symptoms, investigation results, medicines, history.
  3. Group related data and identify nursing diagnoses/problems (e.g. impaired gas exchange, fluid volume excess, activity intolerance, anxiety).
  4. Link each problem to its supporting data with arrows and labels; show relationships between problems.
  5. Under each problem, write nursing interventions with rationale.
  6. Write expected outcomes and evaluation for each problem.
  7. Review and revise the map as the patient's condition changes.

Uses

  • Planning and organising individualised, holistic nursing care.
  • Teaching pathophysiology and linking it with signs, symptoms and care.
  • Pre- and post-clinical conference discussions.
  • Assessment of students' understanding and reasoning.

Advantages

  • Develops critical thinking and clinical reasoning; shows the "big picture".
  • Promotes meaningful rather than rote learning; integrates theory and practice.
  • Visual and easy to review; helps identify gaps and misconceptions.
  • Takes less writing time than long care plans and encourages creativity.

Limitations – initially difficult and time-consuming; can become cluttered; evaluation needs clear rubrics.

Role of the teacher – explains the method with examples, provides templates, reviews maps and asks questions about links, gives feedback using a rubric (accuracy of data, relevance of diagnoses, logical links, appropriateness of interventions).

Conclusion Concept mapping, based on Novak's work, is a visual strategy in which students link a patient's data, nursing diagnoses, interventions and outcomes; it develops critical thinking, holistic care planning and meaningful learning in the clinical area.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the characteristics of an effective clinical teacher.
answer_html:
Introduction The clinical teacher guides students in applying knowledge to real patients. Research on nursing students' perceptions shows that effective clinical teachers combine clinical competence, teaching ability, good relationships, a positive personality and fair evaluation.

Characteristics 1. Clinical (nursing) competence

  • Sound, updated knowledge and expert clinical skills; able to demonstrate procedures correctly.
  • Good clinical judgement; practises evidence-based, safe and ethical care.

  • Acts as a role model of professional behaviour – caring, respectful and accountable. 2. Teaching ability

  • Plans clinical experiences according to objectives and students' levels.

  • Explains clearly, links theory with practice, demonstrates and supervises.
  • Uses questioning to stimulate thinking; encourages problem-solving and independence.
  • Conducts clinical conferences, bedside clinics and rounds effectively.

  • Provides timely, specific, constructive feedback. 3. Interpersonal relationships

  • Approachable, supportive and respectful; shows genuine interest in students.

  • Creates a non-threatening atmosphere where students can ask questions and admit mistakes.
  • Avoids criticising or embarrassing students in front of patients or staff.

  • Maintains good relations with ward staff, doctors and patients; coordinates students' activities with the ward. 4. Personal qualities

  • Enthusiasm, patience, sense of humour, flexibility, honesty, punctuality and self-confidence.

  • Emotional stability; calm in emergencies. 5. Evaluation skills

  • Fair, objective and consistent evaluation using clear criteria (checklists, rating scales).

  • Shares evaluation with students and helps them improve. 6. Availability and supervision

  • Present and accessible in the clinical area; supervises closely at first and gradually allows independence.

  • Ensures patient safety while allowing students to learn. 7. Professional development

  • Keeps up to date, participates in research and continuing education, and contributes to quality improvement.

Roles of the clinical teacher – planner, facilitator, role model, supervisor, evaluator, counsellor, liaison between college and hospital, patient advocate and researcher.

Behaviours students describe as ineffective – being unavailable, criticising in public, intimidating or sarcastic remarks, unclear expectations, unfair evaluation and lack of interest in teaching; an effective teacher consciously avoids these.

Self-development of the clinical teacher – seeking feedback from students and ward staff, reflecting on teaching encounters, observing experienced colleagues, attending faculty development programmes and maintaining clinical practice hours help a teacher remain effective in the clinical area.

Conclusion An effective clinical teacher is clinically competent, a good teacher and role model, approachable and supportive, enthusiastic and patient, fair in evaluation, available for supervision and committed to patient safety and professional growth.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the practice models for clinical teaching – preceptorship, mentorship and the dedicated education unit.
answer_html:
Introduction Practice models describe how clinical education is organised – who supervises students and how the college and the clinical agency share responsibility. Common models are the traditional faculty-supervised model, preceptorship, mentorship and the dedicated education unit.

1. Traditional (faculty-supervised) model

  • A college faculty member supervises a group of students (e.g. 8–10) in a ward.
  • Advantages – the teacher knows the curriculum and objectives.
  • Limitations – limited individual supervision; the faculty member may be less familiar with the ward; students may be seen as outsiders.

2. Preceptorship model

  • A preceptor is an experienced, competent staff nurse in the clinical agency who is assigned to guide one student (one-to-one) for a defined period, usually in the final year or internship.
  • The college faculty coordinates, prepares preceptors and evaluates with them.
  • Roles of the preceptor – orientation to the unit, role model, teacher of skills, supervisor, evaluator, socialiser into the professional role.
  • Advantages – individual attention; real-world practice; smoother transition from student to staff nurse; improved confidence and competence; benefits for the preceptor's professional growth.
  • Challenges – preceptors' workload; need for preparation and recognition; variable quality.

3. Mentorship model

  • A mentor is an experienced professional who supports a less experienced person (mentee) in a long-term relationship focused on personal and professional development – guidance, advice, encouragement and career planning.
  • In colleges, each faculty member may mentor a group of students throughout the programme (mentor–mentee system).
  • Difference – preceptorship is short-term and focused on clinical skills in a specific area; mentorship is long-term, broader and focused on overall development.

4. Dedicated education unit (DEU)

  • A clinical unit (ward) developed jointly by the college and the hospital as an optimal learning environment, where staff nurses are trained as clinical teachers (clinical instructors) and work with students, while college faculty act as coordinators and support the staff.
  • Advantages – a consistent, supportive learning environment; staff committed to teaching; better integration of education and practice; improved quality of care.
  • Requirements – strong partnership, training of staff, mutual commitment.

5. Other models

  • Clinical teaching associate / joint appointment model – nurses who hold positions in both the hospital and the college.
  • Internship – a period of supervised practice after course completion, such as the internship in the final year of the B.Sc Nursing programme.
  • Nurse residency programmes for new graduates.

Conclusion Practice models for clinical teaching include the traditional faculty-supervised model, preceptorship (short-term one-to-one clinical guidance by a staff nurse), mentorship (long-term developmental relationship) and the dedicated education unit (a partnership ward where trained staff teach students); good models improve supervision, integration of theory and practice, and transition to professional roles.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the clinical conference as a clinical teaching method.
answer_html:
Definition A clinical conference is a group discussion of students with the clinical teacher (and sometimes ward staff), held in the clinical setting, about patients, their care and students' experiences, to promote problem-solving and application of theory to practice.

Purposes

  • To plan nursing care and share information about patients.
  • To analyse clinical experiences, problems and feelings.
  • To develop critical thinking, problem-solving and communication skills.
  • To link theory with practice and to learn from each other's experiences.
  • To provide feedback and evaluation.

Types

  1. Pre-clinical (pre-conference) – held at the beginning of the shift (10–20 minutes); students present their patient assignments, plans of care and priorities; the teacher clarifies doubts and checks preparedness.
  2. Post-clinical (post-conference) – held at the end of the shift (30–60 minutes); students discuss what they did, problems faced, how they were solved, feelings and learning; the teacher summarises and gives feedback.
  3. Nursing care conference – an in-depth discussion of the care of one patient presented by a student (sometimes with the patient present, with consent).
  4. Topic (issue) conference – discussion of a specific topic or issue arising in the ward, e.g. medication errors, pressure ulcer prevention, ethical issues.
  5. Interdisciplinary conference – with doctors, physiotherapists and others.

Organisation (steps)

  1. Planning – fix the time, place (a quiet room near the ward), topic or patients; inform students and ward in-charge.
  2. Preparation by students – study the patient's records, assess the patient, prepare care plans or points for discussion.
  3. Conduct – the teacher acts as a facilitator; students present; the group asks questions and discusses; the teacher guides with questions and adds information.
  4. Summary – key learning points are summarised.
  5. Evaluation – participation, quality of presentation and reasoning; feedback.

Advantages

  • Encourages reflection and peer learning; students learn about patients they did not care for.
  • Develops reasoning, presentation and communication skills.
  • Provides a forum to express feelings (e.g. after a patient's death) and receive support.
  • Helps the teacher assess understanding and give feedback.

Limitations

  • Needs time and a suitable place; ward workload may interfere.
  • Some students may not participate; discussion may become superficial without good facilitation.
  • Confidentiality of patient information must be maintained.

Conclusion Clinical conferences – pre-clinical, post-clinical, nursing care, topic and interdisciplinary – are planned group discussions in the clinical area that help students plan care, analyse experiences, develop critical thinking and learn from each other under the guidance of the clinical teacher.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: What is a nursing round?
answer_html: A nursing round is a planned visit by a group of students (with the clinical teacher or nurse manager) to selected patients in the ward to observe, discuss and evaluate their conditions and nursing care. Purposes – to learn about different patients and conditions, compare care, develop observation and problem-solving skills, and evaluate the quality of care. Types – teaching rounds (for students), nursing care rounds (to review care), grand rounds (a selected patient presented to a larger audience) and managerial rounds by the nursing superintendent. Steps – select patients and obtain consent; brief the group; visit and present each patient (history, condition, nursing care) briefly without disturbing the patient; discuss sensitive matters away from the bedside; summarise learning.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: What is a bedside clinic?
answer_html:
A bedside clinic is a clinical teaching method in which a small group of students learns at the patient's bedside, under the guidance of the teacher.

  • A student (or the teacher) presents the patient's history and condition; with the patient's consent, the group observes or examines the patient; the group then discusses the findings, nursing problems and care, preferably away from the bedside if sensitive. Purposes – to learn assessment and nursing care from real patients, link theory with practice, and develop observation, communication and clinical reasoning. Precautions – respect privacy and dignity, avoid tiring the patient, avoid frightening medical terms at the bedside and maintain confidentiality.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: What are the methods of patient assignment in clinical teaching?
answer_html:
Patient assignment is the allocation of patients or nursing activities to students for clinical learning. Methods

  1. Case method (total patient care) – a student gives complete care to one or more patients.
  2. Functional method – a student carries out particular tasks for many patients (e.g. medicines, vital signs).
  3. Team method – a group of students works under a team leader to care for a group of patients.
  4. Primary nursing – a student is responsible for a patient's care throughout the stay, under supervision. Criteria – learning objectives, student's level and competence, patient's condition and needs, continuity of care, workload and safety.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: (a) Define educational media and explain their purposes, principles and steps of use. (6 marks) (b) Classify audiovisual aids. (3 marks) (c) Describe the projected aids, with their preparation, use, advantages and limitations. (6 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definition, purposes, principles and steps (6 marks) Definition

  • Educational (teaching) media are the materials, devices and channels used to convey instructional messages from the teacher to the learner, so that learning becomes clear, interesting and effective.
  • Audiovisual (AV) aids are instructional devices that help the learner to hear and/or see what is being taught – "aids" to teaching, not substitutes for the teacher.

Purposes

  1. Attract and hold attention; arouse interest and motivation.
  2. Make abstract ideas concrete and easy to understand (e.g. anatomy through models).
  3. Save time and help explain complex processes (e.g. the cardiac cycle through animation).
  4. Use several senses – multisensory learning improves understanding and retention.
  5. Provide realistic experiences that cannot be brought to the class (e.g. a video of a surgical procedure).
  6. Encourage active participation, discussion and thinking.
  7. Overcome language barriers and suit different learning styles.
  8. Standardise teaching across groups and support self-learning.
  9. Reinforce and review learning.

Components of media use – the message (content), the medium (device or material), the learner, the teacher and the environment in which it is used.

Principles of selection

  • Relevance to objectives and content.
  • Suitability to the learners' age, level, number and background.
  • Accuracy and up-to-date content; scientific correctness.
  • Simplicity and clarity – one main idea, easily seen or heard by all.
  • Cost-effectiveness and availability; locally available materials preferred.
  • Practicability – ease of handling, portability, availability of electricity and equipment.
  • Variety – avoid over-reliance on one type.

Principles of use

  • Prepare and check the aid and equipment in advance; arrange the room (lighting, seating, screen).
  • Introduce the aid and its purpose; display it only when needed and remove it afterwards to avoid distraction.
  • Position it so that all learners can see and hear; stand aside so as not to block the view.
  • Explain while showing; encourage observation and questions.
  • Do not overload – few aids, used purposefully; the aid supports, not replaces, teaching.
  • Evaluate its effectiveness and maintain it properly after use.

Steps of using media (ASSURE model)

  1. Analyse learners – characteristics, competencies, learning styles.
  2. State objectives.
  3. Select methods, media and materials.
  4. Utilise media and materials – preview, prepare the environment and learners, present.
  5. Require learner participation – practice, discussion, feedback.
  6. Evaluate and revise – learners' achievement and the effectiveness of media.

(b) Classification of AV aids (3 marks) 1. According to the senses involved

  • Audio aids – radio, audio recordings, podcasts, public address systems, telephone.
  • Visual aids – boards, charts, posters, graphs, diagrams, pictures, flash cards, models, specimens, slides, transparencies.

  • Audiovisual aids – films, video, television, multimedia computer presentations, video conferencing, virtual reality. 2. According to projection

  • Non-projected aids – chalkboard, whiteboard, flannel board, bulletin board, flip charts, charts, posters, graphs, cartoons, flash cards, photographs, models, specimens, realia, puppets, exhibitions.

  • Projected aids – overhead projector, slide projector, opaque projector, LCD/multimedia projector, document camera, film projector. 3. According to motion

  • Still visuals – pictures, charts, slides, transparencies.

  • Moving visuals – films, video, animation. 4. Other groups

  • Realia and models – real objects and three-dimensional replicas.

  • Electronic and computer-based media – computer-assisted learning, simulation, virtual reality, online resources, mobile technology.
  • Activity aids – demonstrations, field trips, dramatisation, exhibitions.

(c) Projected aids (6 marks) Projected aids use light to project an enlarged image onto a screen so that a large group can see it.

1. Overhead projector (OHP)

  • Description – projects images from transparencies (transparent sheets) placed on a horizontal glass stage, through a lens and mirror, onto a screen behind the teacher.
  • Preparation – write or draw on transparencies with permanent or water-soluble markers, or print them; use large lettering (at least 6 mm), few lines (6–8) per sheet and colours; number the transparencies.
  • Use – place the projector so that the image is square and focused; face the class while pointing on the transparency with a pen; use masking (revealing points one by one) and overlays (building complex diagrams).
  • Advantages – used in a lit room; the teacher faces the class; can be prepared in advance or written during the class; simple and inexpensive.
  • Limitations – needs electricity; bulb may fuse; "keystone" distortion if not aligned; now largely replaced by LCD projectors.

2. Slide projector

  • Description – projects 35 mm photographic slides placed in a tray or carousel; slides can show photographs of patients, conditions and procedures.
  • Use – arrange slides in order, test the projector, darken the room partly, explain each slide.
  • Advantages – high-quality, realistic images; can be rearranged and reused.
  • Limitations – a darkened room makes note-taking difficult; slides are costly to prepare; mostly replaced by digital images.

3. LCD/multimedia projector and computer presentation (e.g. PowerPoint)

  • Description – connects to a computer or laptop and projects text, pictures, animations, audio and video onto a screen; interactive smart boards allow writing and touch control.
  • Preparation of slides
    • One main idea per slide; about 6 lines of 6 words ("6 × 6 rule").
    • Large, clear fonts (headings 32–44 point, text 24 point or more) and high contrast.
    • Relevant images and diagrams; minimal animation.
    • Accurate content with references.
  • Use – check the connection and display beforehand; face the audience; do not read from the slides; use a remote or pointer; pause for questions; keep a backup copy.
  • Advantages – combines several media; easy to prepare, edit, store and share; attractive; suitable for large audiences and online teaching.
  • Limitations – dependence on electricity and equipment; technical failures; "death by PowerPoint" when overused; can make teaching teacher-centred.

4. Document camera (visualiser) and opaque projector

  • Projects images of books, pictures, objects or handwritten notes directly, without preparing transparencies; useful for demonstrating small objects, instruments and drug labels to a whole class.

5. Film and video projection – films and videos projected through a projector or screen show procedures, real situations and processes in motion (e.g. normal delivery, hand washing); the teacher should introduce the film, stop at key points for discussion and follow up afterwards.

Care of projected aids – cover the equipment when not in use, allow the bulb to cool before moving, keep lenses clean, store in a dry place, handle cables carefully and keep spare bulbs and fuses.

Low-cost and locally made aids – when resources are limited, teachers can prepare effective aids from locally available materials: charts and flash cards from chart paper, models from clay, thermocol or cardboard, flannel-board cut-outs, puppets, and real objects from the ward. Such aids are cheap, culturally familiar and easy to replace, and students can be involved in preparing them, which itself is a learning experience.

Conclusion Educational media are materials and devices that carry instructional messages; they attract attention, make learning concrete and multisensory, and improve retention when selected and used on sound principles (such as the ASSURE model). AV aids are classified as audio, visual and audiovisual, projected and non-projected, still and moving. Projected aids – the overhead projector, slide projector, LCD/multimedia projector, document camera and film projection – enlarge images for groups, each with its preparation, use, advantages and limitations.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the board devices used in teaching – chalkboard, whiteboard, flannel board, bulletin board and smart board.
answer_html:
1. Chalkboard (blackboard)

  • The oldest and most widely available visual aid – a dark green or black surface on which the teacher writes with chalk.
  • Principles of use
    • Plan the board work in advance; divide the board into sections.
    • Write legibly, in large letters, from left to right, top to bottom; use coloured chalk for emphasis.
    • Stand to one side while writing; face the class while explaining; do not talk to the board.
    • Draw simple diagrams; erase unnecessary matter; leave the board clean.
  • Advantages – cheap, always available, flexible, useful for spontaneous explanations, summaries and diagrams.
  • Limitations – chalk dust (allergy), limited space, work is lost when erased, writing takes class time, poor legibility with bad handwriting.

2. Whiteboard (marker board)

  • A white glossy surface used with dry-erase markers; dust-free and gives bright colours; also usable as a projection screen.
  • Limitations – markers dry quickly and are costly; glare; ghost marks if not cleaned.

3. Flannel board (flannelgraph)

  • A board covered with flannel or felt cloth; pictures, symbols and words backed with sandpaper or flannel stick to it and can be moved.
  • Uses – building up a story or sequence step by step (e.g. the food groups, the stages of fetal development, steps of hand washing), especially for health education.
  • Advantages – low cost, attractive, materials can be reused and rearranged; encourages participation.
  • Limitations – pieces may fall off; suitable for small groups.

4. Bulletin board (notice board)

  • A board made of soft wood, cork or soft board on which notices, pictures, charts, news cuttings and displays are pinned.
  • Uses – display of information on a theme (World Health Day, infection control), announcements, students' work, recent advances.
  • Principles – one theme at a time, an attractive caption, balance and colour, regular change (weekly), placed at eye level in a frequently visited place.

5. Smart board (interactive whiteboard)

  • A touch-sensitive board connected to a computer and projector; the teacher can write, draw, move objects, play videos, open websites and save the notes.
  • Advantages – interactive and attractive; combines many media; notes can be saved and shared.
  • Limitations – costly; needs electricity, training and maintenance.

6. Magnetic board – a metal board on which items with small magnets are moved (useful for planning, e.g. ward assignments).

Care – keep boards clean and dry; use proper erasers and cleaners; repaint chalkboards when shiny; replace felt when worn.

Conclusion Board devices – chalkboard, whiteboard, flannel board, bulletin board, magnetic board and smart board – are simple to sophisticated visual aids that support explanation, summarising and display when used with planning, legibility, clear layout and care.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the preparation and use of charts, graphs, posters and cartoons as teaching aids.
answer_html:
1. Charts

  • Definition – a visual combination of drawings, pictures, words, numbers or diagrams on a sheet, used to present information clearly and systematically.
  • Types
    • Flow chart – steps of a process (e.g. the referral system, steps of CPR).
    • Tabular chart – information in rows and columns (e.g. immunisation schedule).
    • Tree chart – development or branches from a common source (e.g. classification of drugs).
    • Organisational chart – structure of an organisation (e.g. the nursing service hierarchy).
    • Pictorial chart – mainly pictures (e.g. sources of iron).
    • Flip chart – a series of charts bound at the top and flipped one by one to present a sequence (useful in health talks).
  • Principles of preparation
    • One main idea per chart; simple, clear title; a few words.
    • Large letters (visible from the back – at least 2.5 cm high for a classroom).
    • Suitable colours and contrast; good layout with balance and white space.
    • Accurate, up-to-date information.
    • Size suited to the group (standard sheets of about 50 × 75 cm).
  • Use – display at eye level when needed; point to parts while explaining; remove after use.

2. Graphs

  • Definition – visual presentation of numerical data showing relationships, comparisons and trends.
  • Types
    • Bar graph – comparison of quantities (e.g. immunisation coverage in different districts).
    • Line graph – trends over time (e.g. IMR over 20 years, temperature chart).
    • Pie chart – proportions of a whole (e.g. causes of maternal deaths).
    • Pictogram – pictures representing numbers.
    • Histogram and frequency polygon – distribution of continuous data.
  • Principles – a title, labelled axes and units, a legend, simple scales, accurate data and the source of data.

3. Posters

  • Definition – a large, bold, attractive visual with a single message and few words, designed to catch attention quickly and motivate action ("a poster is a visual shout").
  • Characteristics of a good poster
    • One idea; short slogan; bold, simple pictures; bright contrasting colours.
    • Readable from a distance; culturally appropriate; tells "what to do".
    • Example: "Wash hands – save lives" with a picture of hand washing.
  • Use – displayed in wards, OPDs, schools and community places; changed frequently.

4. Cartoons

  • Definition – humorous or exaggerated drawings, often with a caption, that convey a message quickly.
