  • Uses – to attract attention, simplify an idea, make a point about behaviour (e.g. dangers of self-medication, tobacco use) and stimulate discussion.
  • Precautions – must be understood by the audience, avoid offending any group, keep the message clear.

Advantages of these aids – inexpensive, easy to prepare with local materials, reusable, no electricity needed, attract attention and simplify information. Limitations – limited detail, may become outdated, can be damaged, small sizes are not visible in large groups.

Conclusion Charts (flow, tabular, tree, organisational, pictorial, flip), graphs (bar, line, pie, pictogram, histogram), posters and cartoons are simple, inexpensive visual aids that present information, data and messages clearly when prepared with one main idea, large lettering, good colours, accuracy and proper display.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the use of models, specimens and realia in nursing education.
answer_html:
1. Realia (real objects)

  • Meaning – actual objects used in teaching – instruments, equipment, drugs, food items, contraceptives, dressing materials.
  • Examples – showing a real IV cannula, urinary catheter, sphygmomanometer, oral contraceptive pill packet, samples of iron-rich foods.
  • Advantages – the most concrete experience (top of the "direct experience" level in Dale's cone); students can see, touch and handle them; links directly to practice.
  • Limitations – some objects are too large, small, rare, costly or dangerous to bring into class.

2. Models

  • Meaning – three-dimensional representations of real objects, which may be smaller, larger or the same size as the original.
  • Types
    • Solid models – show external form (e.g. a model of the heart or kidney).
    • Cut-away and sectional models – show internal structure (e.g. a cross-section of skin, eye or ear).
    • Working models – show functioning (e.g. a model of the lungs and diaphragm showing breathing).
    • Scale models – enlarged or reduced (e.g. an enlarged model of a cell or tooth).
    • Mock-ups – simplified representations of real situations (e.g. a model kitchen or a sanitary latrine).
    • Manikins and task trainers – life-size models for practising procedures (CPR manikin, IV arm, injection pad, delivery and episiotomy models, catheterisation models).
    • Simulators – computerised manikins that respond physiologically.
  • Advantages
    • Make abstract structures concrete; three-dimensional and can be handled.
    • Allow repeated practice of procedures without risk to patients.
    • Durable and reusable; useful for demonstration and return demonstration.
  • Limitations – may not show exact proportions or textures; costly (especially simulators); can break; may give a false sense of competence.

3. Specimens

  • Meaning – real biological materials preserved for study – anatomical and pathological specimens (e.g. a preserved fetus, placenta, diseased organs), skeleton and bones, slides of parasites, insect specimens (mosquitoes, flies).
  • Uses – anatomy and pathology teaching, community health (vectors), obstetrics (placenta, fetal skull).
  • Care – preserved in formalin in sealed jars with labels; handled with gloves; kept in a museum or laboratory with proper records; ethical respect for human specimens.

Principles of use

  • Select according to objectives; show at the right time; make sure all students can see (pass around or use small groups).
  • Explain parts and relationships; allow students to handle and practise under supervision.
  • Combine with charts, videos and real clinical experience.
  • Clean, store and maintain properly after use; keep an inventory.

Conclusion Realia, models (solid, cut-away, working, scale, mock-ups, manikins, simulators) and specimens provide concrete, three-dimensional experiences that make structures and procedures easy to understand and practise; they must be selected, used and maintained carefully.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain computer simulation, virtual reality and mobile technology as teaching media.
answer_html:
1. Computer-based learning resources and computer simulation

  • Computer-assisted learning (CAL) – tutorials, drill-and-practice programmes and interactive e-modules with immediate feedback.
  • Computer (screen-based) simulation – software that presents virtual patients whose condition changes according to the learner's decisions (e.g. managing a patient with chest pain or DKA), and serious games for drug calculation, triage or infection control.
  • Advantages – safe practice of clinical decision-making; repeated attempts; immediate feedback; self-paced; standardised scenarios; can be used anywhere.
  • Limitations – does not develop hands-on skills; cost of software; needs computers and internet.

2. Virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR)

  • Virtual reality – a computer-generated, three-dimensional, immersive environment experienced through a head-mounted display (headset) and controllers; the learner feels "present" in the situation (e.g. a virtual operating theatre, a home visit, the inside of the heart).
  • Augmented reality – digital images superimposed on the real world through a phone, tablet or glasses (e.g. 3-D anatomy over a manikin, vein visualisation).
  • Uses – anatomy, procedures (IV cannulation, catheterisation), emergency response, disaster drills, empathy training (experiencing life with visual impairment or dementia).
  • Advantages – highly engaging; realistic, safe repetition; improves spatial understanding and confidence.
  • Limitations – costly equipment; motion sickness in some users; needs technical support; limited content in local contexts.

3. Mobile technology (m-learning)

  • Meaning – learning through smartphones and tablets.
  • Examples
    • Drug-reference and clinical calculator apps; anatomy apps.
    • Flashcard and quiz apps; podcasts and short videos.
    • Learning management system apps; messaging groups for class communication.
    • QR codes on skill-lab stations linking to procedure videos.
    • E-books and digital logbooks.
  • Advantages – learning anytime, anywhere; quick access at the point of care; suits today's learners; supports microlearning and self-directed learning.
  • Limitations – distraction and misuse; unreliable sources; small screens; privacy risks if patient information is photographed or shared; unequal access to devices and data.

Guidelines and role of the teacher

  • Select reliable, evidence-based software and apps; align them with learning outcomes.
  • Prepare students (orientation) and integrate these media with classroom, skill-lab and clinical teaching.
  • Debrief after simulations and VR sessions.
  • Set rules for responsible use – no photographing of patients, protecting confidentiality, avoiding social-media sharing of clinical information.
  • Evaluate effectiveness and ensure equal access.

Conclusion Computer simulation, virtual and augmented reality and mobile technology are modern teaching media that provide interactive, immersive and flexible learning and safe practice of decision-making, but need investment, guidance, ethical use and integration with hands-on clinical learning.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain audio aids and video and films as teaching aids.
answer_html:
1. Audio aids

  • Meaning – aids that use only the sense of hearing.
  • Types
    • Radio – educational broadcasts and health programmes.
    • Audio recordings and podcasts – lectures, heart and lung sounds, interviews, patients' narratives.
    • Public address system and microphones – for large groups.
    • Telephone and audio conferencing – for distance teaching and consultation.
    • Language laboratory for communication skills.
  • Advantages – inexpensive and widely available; useful for distance learning and listening skills (e.g. auscultation sounds); can be replayed; useful for learners with visual impairment.
  • Limitations – one-way; attention may wander; no visual support; recording quality may be poor.

2. Video and films

  • Meaning – audiovisual aids that present moving pictures with sound, showing events, processes and procedures as they actually happen.
  • Types – educational films and documentaries; recorded procedure videos (e.g. CPR, normal delivery, sterile dressing); recorded lectures; television programmes; animations; video recordings of students' own performance (for feedback); online video platforms.
  • Steps in using a film or video
    1. Select and preview – relevant to objectives, accurate, of suitable length (preferably 10–20 minutes), suitable language.
    2. Prepare the room and equipment – screen, sound, seating, lighting; check playback.
    3. Introduce – purpose of the film, points to observe, questions to keep in mind.
    4. Show – pause at key points to explain or ask questions.
    5. Follow-up discussion – clarify doubts, summarise learning, link to practice; assignments.
    6. Evaluate – learners' understanding and the usefulness of the film.
  • Advantages
    • Show real situations and motion that cannot be brought to class (surgery, deliveries, community conditions).
    • Arouse interest and emotions; influence attitudes (e.g. a film on the effects of tobacco).
    • Standardise demonstrations; can be repeated, paused and slowed down.
    • Video recording of students' performance gives objective feedback.
  • Limitations – costly to produce; need equipment and electricity; may be passive "entertainment" without discussion; content may not suit local conditions; some films become outdated.

Example – before teaching the "neonatal resuscitation" session, the teacher shows a five-minute procedure video, pauses at each step to ask "What should be done next?", and then the students practise on the manikin – combining the video with active practice.

Conclusion Audio aids (radio, recordings, podcasts, PA systems, telephone) use hearing alone, while video and films combine sight, sound and motion to show real procedures and situations; both are effective when previewed, introduced, shown with pauses and followed by discussion and evaluation.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: What is the use of telecommunication in education?
answer_html:
Telecommunication is the transmission of information over a distance by telephone, radio, television, satellite, computer networks and the internet. Uses in education (tele-education/distance education)

  • Live virtual classes and video conferencing – teaching students in many centres at the same time; guest lectures by experts from distant places.
  • Webinars, online courses and recorded lectures – continuing nursing education.
  • Satellite-based education channels and educational broadcasting.
  • Tele-consultation and tele-mentoring for clinical guidance. Advantages – reaches learners in remote areas; saves travel time and cost; access to experts; flexible learning. Limitations – needs reliable internet and equipment; less personal interaction; technical problems.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: What is Edgar Dale's cone of experience?
answer_html: Edgar Dale's cone of experience (1946) is a visual model that arranges learning experiences from the most concrete (at the base) to the most abstract (at the top). Levels (from base to top) – direct purposeful experiences → contrived experiences (models, simulations) → dramatised experiences (role play) → demonstrations → field trips → exhibits → motion pictures/television → recordings, radio and still pictures → visual symbols (charts, graphs) → verbal symbols (words). Significance – learners gain more from concrete, multisensory and active experiences; teachers should choose aids that move from concrete to abstract, combining several levels, especially for beginners.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: State the guidelines for preparing an effective PowerPoint presentation.
answer_html:
Guidelines

  1. One main idea per slide; follow the 6 × 6 rule – not more than about six lines and six words per line.
  2. Large, clear fonts – headings 32–44 point, text at least 24 point; simple font styles.
  3. High contrast – dark text on a light background (or the reverse); avoid busy backgrounds.
  4. Use relevant pictures, diagrams and graphs instead of long text; cite sources.
  5. Minimal animation and sound effects; consistent design throughout.
  6. Check spelling and accuracy.
  7. Do not read the slides – speak to the audience; use the slides as cues.
  8. Rehearse; check equipment beforehand; keep a backup copy; allow time for questions.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: (a) Define measurement, assessment and evaluation. (3 marks) (b) Explain the purposes, scope and principles of selecting assessment methods. (6 marks) (c) Describe the barriers to evaluation and the guidelines for developing assessment tests. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Blueprint (table of specifications) for a test
labels: rows – units or topics with weightage by teaching hours; columns – levels of learning (knowledge
with marks in each cell adding to the total

answer_html:
(a) Definitions (3 marks)

  • Measurement – the process of assigning numbers or quantities to a characteristic according to rules (e.g. a student scored 36 out of 50). It is quantitative and answers "how much".
  • Assessment – the systematic process of collecting, reviewing and using information about learners' learning (knowledge, skills and attitudes) to improve learning and make decisions; it uses tests, observation, assignments, portfolios and other methods.
  • Evaluation – the process of making a value judgement about the worth, quality or effectiveness of learning, a teacher, a course or a programme, based on measurement and assessment against criteria. It is qualitative and quantitative and answers "how good".
  • Relationship – evaluation = measurement/assessment + value judgement.

Types of evaluation

  • Placement – before instruction, to place students appropriately.
  • Formative – during instruction, to give feedback and improve learning (class tests, quizzes, clinical feedback).
  • Diagnostic – to identify learning difficulties and their causes.
  • Summative – at the end of a course, to grade, certify or promote (end-semester examination).
  • Norm-referenced – compares a student with others (rank in class); criterion-referenced – compares performance with a fixed standard (competency achieved or not).

(b) Purposes, scope and principles (6 marks) Purposes

  1. To determine the extent to which learning outcomes are achieved.
  2. To give feedback to students about strengths and weaknesses and to motivate them.
  3. To diagnose learning difficulties and plan remedial teaching.
  4. To grade, promote, certify and select students (e.g. for awards, higher studies, employment).
  5. To ensure safe and competent practice before students care for patients independently.
  6. To give feedback to teachers about the effectiveness of teaching methods and to improve them.
  7. To evaluate the curriculum and programme and provide data for revision and accreditation.
  8. To provide information to parents, employers and regulatory bodies.
  9. To predict future performance and guide students.

Scope

  • Cognitive – knowledge, understanding, application, analysis and problem-solving (written and oral tests).
  • Psychomotor – clinical and procedural skills (observation, OSCE/OSPE, simulation).
  • Affective – attitudes, values and professional behaviour (attitude scales, observation, anecdotal records, self-evaluation).
  • Communication – written (care plans, reports) and verbal (oral examination, case presentations).
  • Learners, teachers, courses, programmes and institutions – all can be evaluated.

Principles of selecting assessment methods

  1. Alignment with learning outcomes – the method must measure what the objective states (e.g. a skill is assessed by observation, not an essay).
  2. Validity – measures what it intends to measure.
  3. Reliability – gives consistent results.
  4. Objectivity – scoring is not affected by the examiner's personal opinion.
  5. Comprehensiveness and balance – covers all important content and domains; uses multiple methods.
  6. Continuity – evaluation is a continuous process, combining formative and summative assessment.
  7. Practicability (usability) – feasible in terms of time, cost, staff and resources.
  8. Fairness – equal opportunity for all students; transparent criteria shared in advance.
  9. Discrimination – distinguishes between good and poor performers.
  10. Educational value – assessment should promote learning ("assessment drives learning") and provide feedback.
  11. Ethics – confidentiality, honesty and respect for students and patients.

(c) Barriers to evaluation and guidelines for developing tests (6 marks) Barriers to evaluation

  • Examiner-related
    • Halo effect – a general impression influences the rating of specific items.
    • Leniency or severity error – rating everyone too high or too low.
    • Central tendency error – avoiding extremes and rating everyone as average.
    • Personal bias, prejudice and favouritism; fatigue; inconsistency between examiners.
  • Tool-related – poorly constructed questions, ambiguous wording, unclear criteria, tests that measure only recall.
  • Student-related – examination anxiety, illness, cheating, coaching for the test.
  • Situation-related – variation in clinical situations and patients, noise, time pressure, lack of resources.
  • Organisational – large numbers of students, shortage of faculty, lack of training in evaluation, over-emphasis on final examinations.
  • Ethical – breach of confidentiality, unfair practices.

Guidelines for developing assessment tests

  1. Determine the purpose of the test (formative, summative, diagnostic).
  2. Review learning outcomes and content to be tested.
  3. Prepare a blueprint (table of specifications) – distribute marks across units (according to their weightage, e.g. teaching hours), levels of learning (knowledge, understanding, application) and types of questions.
  4. Select appropriate item types – essay, short answer, MCQ, practical stations – matching outcomes.
  5. Write items carefully
    • Clear, unambiguous language; one idea per item; appropriate difficulty.
    • Avoid clues, tricks and negative wording; ensure independence of items.
  6. Prepare the answer key and marking scheme (model answers with marks for each point; checklists for practical stations).
  7. Assemble the test – group similar items, arrange from easy to difficult, give clear instructions, marks and time.
  8. Review and moderate – by colleagues for accuracy, coverage and language.
  9. Administer under standard conditions; ensure security and fairness.
  10. Score objectively using the key; have double marking or moderation for essays.
  11. Analyse results – item analysis (difficulty and discrimination indices), reliability; identify poor items.
  12. Give feedback to students and revise the test and teaching; maintain a question bank.

Steps in the evaluation process

  1. Identify the purpose of evaluation and the decisions to be made.
  2. Define the learning outcomes or standards to be evaluated.
  3. Select or construct suitable tools – tests, checklists, rating scales, OSCE stations.
  4. Collect information under fair, standard conditions.
  5. Score and analyse the data (marks, grades, item analysis).
  6. Interpret and make judgements – compare with criteria or norms.
  7. Communicate results and give feedback to students and others concerned.
  8. Use the results for improvement – remedial teaching, revision of methods, tests and curriculum.

Grading and the credit system – results may be expressed as marks, percentages, letter grades or grade points; under the credit and grading system followed in the INC 2021 curriculum, internal (formative and continuous) assessment and end-semester (summative) examinations together determine the grade for each course. Transparent criteria, timely results and a system for students to view and discuss their evaluation build trust in the evaluation process.

Role of the nurse teacher in evaluation – plans evaluation along with teaching, prepares valid and reliable tools, conducts examinations fairly, scores objectively, maintains confidentiality of results, gives constructive feedback, counsels students who perform poorly, and uses results to improve teaching.

Programme evaluation – besides students, the nursing programme itself is evaluated through results, feedback from students, alumni and employers, inspection by regulatory bodies and accreditation, so that strengths are maintained and weaknesses corrected.

Conclusion Measurement assigns numbers, assessment collects information about learning, and evaluation makes value judgements; evaluation may be placement, formative, diagnostic or summative, norm- or criterion-referenced. Its purposes include judging achievement of outcomes, feedback, diagnosis, certification, ensuring safe practice and improving teaching and curriculum, across cognitive, psychomotor, affective and communication domains. Methods are chosen for alignment, validity, reliability, objectivity, comprehensiveness, continuity, practicability and fairness. Barriers such as rater errors, poor tools and anxiety are reduced by following guidelines – purpose, blueprint, careful item writing, marking schemes, moderation, standard administration, item analysis and feedback.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the assessment of knowledge using essay questions, short-answer questions and multiple-choice questions (single and multiple response), with guidelines for their construction, merits and demerits.

diagram.caption: Parts of a multiple-choice question
labels: stem (a clear question or incomplete statement
options (one key – the correct or best answer – and three plausible distractors)

answer_html:
1. Essay questions Meaning – questions that require the student to write a long answer in his or her own words, organising and expressing ideas. Types

  • Extended-response (open) – freedom in scope and organisation (e.g. "Discuss the role of the nurse in disaster management").
  • Restricted-response – limits the content and length (e.g. "List and explain four complications of diabetes").

  • Structured (modified) essay – broken into parts with marks for each, often based on a patient situation: "(a) Define… (2) (b) Explain the clinical features… (5) (c) Describe the nursing care… (8)". Guidelines for construction

  • Use for higher-order outcomes (explaining, comparing, analysing, planning, evaluating).

  • State the task clearly using precise directive words (list, describe, explain, compare, justify) rather than vague words like "discuss" alone.
  • Indicate marks and expected length for each part; avoid optional questions (they reduce comparability).

  • Prepare a model answer and marking scheme in advance, listing key points and marks. Guidelines for scoring

  • Use analytic scoring (marks for each point) rather than global impressions.

  • Score one question at a time for all students, without looking at names (code numbers).

  • Avoid being influenced by handwriting, language and length; use double marking or moderation where possible. Merits

  • Assesses higher mental abilities – organisation, analysis, synthesis, evaluation, creativity and expression.

  • Easy to prepare; no guessing; encourages good study habits and writing skills. Demerits

  • Limited sampling of content (few questions).

  • Subjective and unreliable scoring – varies between examiners and for the same examiner; halo effect.
  • Time-consuming to answer and score; influenced by handwriting and language skills; "bluffing" is possible.

2. Short-answer questions (SAQs) Meaning – questions that require a brief answer – a word, phrase, sentence, list, definition, diagram or short paragraph. Forms – completion (fill in the blank), definitions, lists, "give reasons", differentiation, short notes, labelling diagrams.

  • Examples:

    • "Define hypertension."
    • "List four signs of dehydration."
    • "Give two reasons why the head end of the bed is raised in heart failure." Guidelines for construction

  • One clear question with one definite answer or a fixed number of points.

  • Specify the number of points expected ("list four…").
  • Avoid copying sentences from textbooks (encourages rote learning).
  • In completion items, place the blank at the end and keep only one blank.

  • Prepare a key with acceptable answers. Merits

  • Covers wider content than essays; easy to prepare.

  • More objective scoring than essays; less guessing than MCQs.

  • Tests recall and understanding efficiently; suitable for many students. Demerits

  • Mostly tests lower-level learning (recall).

  • Scoring can still be subjective when answers vary; spelling and wording issues.
  • Time-consuming to score compared with MCQs.

3. Multiple-choice questions (MCQs) Meaning – objective items in which the student selects the correct or best answer from a list of options. Parts

  • Stem – the question or problem (often a clinical scenario).

  • Options (alternatives) – usually four, including one key (correct or best answer) and three distractors (plausible incorrect options). Types

  • Single best response (one correct answer) – the commonest type.

    • Example: "The first action of a nurse for a patient who suddenly becomes unresponsive is: (a) check blood pressure (b) check responsiveness and breathing and call for help (c) give oxygen (d) inform relatives."
  • Multiple-response (select all that apply) – two or more options are correct; the student must select all the correct ones.
    • Example: "Which of the following are signs of hypoglycaemia? (select all that apply) sweating; tremors; confusion; polyuria; tachycardia."

  • Other forms – true/false, matching, assertion–reason, and scenario-based (case cluster) MCQs. Guidelines for construction

  • Base each item on an important learning outcome; test application and reasoning, not only recall (use clinical scenarios).

  • The stem should be clear, complete and contain the main idea; avoid unnecessary information.
  • Avoid negative wording; if used, highlight it ("NOT", "EXCEPT").
  • Options should be:
    • homogeneous, of similar length and grammatically consistent with the stem;
    • arranged logically (alphabetical or numerical order);
    • placed so that the key's position is random.
  • Distractors must be plausible (common errors or misconceptions).
  • Avoid "all of the above" and "none of the above"; avoid clues (repeated words, absolute terms like "always" or "never", the longest option being correct).
  • Have one clearly correct or best answer, agreed by experts; review items with colleagues.

  • For multiple-response items, state clearly how many to select or that all correct options must be chosen, and decide the scoring rule in advance. Merits

  • Wide sampling of content in a short time; highly objective, reliable and quick scoring (including by computer).

  • Can test application and analysis if well constructed; useful for large groups and competitive examinations.

  • Item analysis improves quality; items can be stored in a question bank. Demerits

  • Guessing is possible (25% chance with four options).

  • Difficult and time-consuming to construct good items, especially plausible distractors.
  • Do not assess the ability to organise and express ideas or skills and attitudes.
  • Poorly written MCQs test only trivial recall; may encourage rote learning.

Comparison in brief

  • Essays assess organisation and higher thinking with low content coverage and subjective scoring.
  • Short-answer questions cover more content with moderate objectivity.
  • MCQs cover wide content with high objectivity but allow guessing and do not test expression.
  • A good examination combines all three, according to a blueprint.

Item analysis of MCQs – after the test, the difficulty index (percentage of students answering correctly) and the discrimination index (how well the item separates high and low scorers) are calculated, and distractors that nobody chooses are revised.

Oral examination (viva voce) – a complementary method

  • The examiner asks questions orally and the student responds; it assesses knowledge, reasoning, communication and the ability to think quickly.
  • Merits – flexibility to probe deeper; immediate clarification; assesses communication and confidence.
  • Demerits – subjective; low reliability; anxiety; limited sampling; examiner bias.
  • Improvements – structured viva with predetermined questions and model answers, more than one examiner, equal time for each student.

Use of question banks and online testing – departments maintain question banks of reviewed items with their difficulty and discrimination indices, and increasingly use computer-based tests that randomise questions and give immediate results.

Choosing the right format – essays are best for explaining, comparing and planning care; short-answer questions for definitions, lists and reasons; MCQs for wide coverage and application in clinical scenarios. Matching the format to the learning outcome is the key to valid assessment, and every format should be reviewed by colleagues before use.

Conclusion Knowledge is assessed through essay questions (extended, restricted and structured – good for higher abilities but subjective), short-answer questions (wider coverage, more objective, mainly recall) and multiple-choice questions (single best and multiple response – wide coverage, objective scoring, risk of guessing). Each must be constructed and scored according to guidelines, and their combination, guided by a blueprint and item analysis, gives a valid and reliable assessment.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the methods of assessing attitude.
answer_html:
Introduction

  • An attitude is a learned, relatively enduring tendency to feel, think and act in a particular way towards persons, objects or ideas.
  • In nursing, attitudes such as respect for patients, empathy, honesty, responsibility, teamwork and professional values are as important as knowledge and skills, but they are difficult to measure because they are internal and can be faked.
  • Several methods are used together.

1. Attitude scales (self-report instruments)

  • Likert scale (Rensis Likert, 1932)
    • A series of statements about an attitude object, each rated on a 5-point scale – strongly agree, agree, undecided, disagree, strongly disagree – scored 5 to 1 (reversed for negative statements); the total score shows the attitude.
    • Example: "Patients with HIV should be cared for with the same respect as other patients."
    • The most commonly used scale; easy to construct and score.
  • Thurstone scale (equal-appearing intervals, 1928) – statements are given scale values by judges; the respondent marks statements he or she agrees with, and the average scale value is the attitude score. Accurate but laborious to construct.
  • Semantic differential scale (Osgood, 1957) – the concept (e.g. "Nursing profession") is rated on 7-point scales between pairs of opposite adjectives (good–bad, valuable–worthless, pleasant–unpleasant).
  • Guttman (cumulative) scale – statements arranged in order of intensity, so that agreeing with a stronger statement implies agreement with milder ones.

2. Observation-based methods

  • Direct observation of behaviour in the clinical area and class – how the student interacts with patients, maintains privacy and dignity, cooperates with others, accepts feedback.
  • Anecdotal records – brief, factual written descriptions of significant incidents of behaviour, recorded soon after they occur, without interpretation in the description part.
  • Rating scales and checklists for professional behaviour – punctuality, grooming, communication, responsibility, ethical conduct (e.g. graded 1–5).
  • Critical incident technique – recording specific incidents of very good or poor behaviour.

3. Interviews and questionnaires – open discussion about values and responses to situations; questionnaires on beliefs and opinions.

4. Reflective writing – reflective journals, essays on ethical dilemmas, and responses to case vignettes reveal values and attitudes.

5. Peer and self-evaluation; 360-degree feedback – evaluation by peers, ward staff and patients, along with self-assessment.

6. Situational and simulation tests – role play and simulation scenarios (e.g. a patient who refuses treatment) to see the student's responses.

Limitations

  • Students may give socially desirable answers (faking).
  • Observation can be subjective (halo effect, bias); attitudes may change with situations.
  • Requires repeated observations over time by several observers.
  • Attitude assessment is mainly formative – used for guidance and feedback rather than for marks alone.

Conclusion Attitudes are assessed through attitude scales (Likert, Thurstone, semantic differential, Guttman), observation tools (anecdotal records, rating scales, checklists, critical incidents), interviews, reflective writing, peer, self- and 360-degree evaluation and simulated situations; multiple methods over time give a fair picture.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the methods of assessing practical (clinical) skills.
answer_html:
Introduction Practical (clinical) skills – performing procedures, assessing patients, planning and giving care, communicating and making decisions – are assessed by observing performance in real or simulated situations, supported by other methods. As described in Miller's pyramid, skills are assessed at the "shows how" (simulation, OSCE) and "does" (workplace) levels.

Methods

  1. Clinical evaluation by direct observation
    • The teacher observes the student giving care in the ward, OPD or community, using:
      • Checklists – lists of steps marked done or not done (e.g. steps of catheterisation).
      • Rating scales – quality of performance graded (e.g. 1–5: poor to excellent) on items such as skill, safety, organisation and communication.
      • Anecdotal records – descriptions of significant incidents.
    • Videotapes – recording performance for later review, feedback and self-assessment.
  2. Assessment of written communication – nursing care plans, case studies and care studies, drug studies, health education plans, reports, records and reflective journals.
  3. Assessment of verbal communication
    • Oral examination (viva voce) – questions about patients, procedures and rationale.
    • Case presentation and clinical conference participation.
  4. Simulation-based assessment – performance on manikins, simulators or standardised patients in a controlled scenario (e.g. CPR, management of PPH).
  5. OSCE/OSPE (objective structured clinical/practical examination) – students rotate through timed stations testing specific skills with standard checklists, giving objective and reliable assessment.
  6. Practical examination – the traditional long case (total care of an assigned patient, with care plan and viva) and short procedures.
  7. Self-evaluation – the student assesses his or her own performance against criteria; develops reflection and responsibility.
  8. Clinical portfolio – a collection of evidence of learning (care plans, reflections, certificates, feedback) over the programme.
  9. Logbooks and competency checklists – records of procedures observed, assisted and performed independently, signed by the supervisor (as required by the INC curriculum).
  10. Peer evaluation and feedback from ward staff and patients.

Principles of skill assessment

  • Clear criteria shared with students in advance.
  • Observation of actual performance in several situations and by more than one examiner.
  • Standardised tools (checklists, rating scales) to improve objectivity.
  • Combine formative feedback with summative assessment.
  • Patient safety first; obtain patients' consent.
  • Assess knowledge, skill and attitude together (competence).

Conclusion Practical skills are assessed through direct observation with checklists, rating scales and anecdotal records, videotapes, written and verbal communication (care plans, viva, case presentations), simulation, OSCE/OSPE, practical examinations, self-evaluation, portfolios, logbooks and feedback from others, using clear criteria and multiple observations.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the objective structured practical examination (OSPE) and objective structured clinical examination (OSCE).
answer_html:
Meaning

  • The objective structured clinical examination (OSCE) was introduced by Ronald Harden (1975), and its adaptation for practical/laboratory skills, the objective structured practical examination (OSPE), by Harden and Cairncross (1980).
  • In both, students rotate through a series of stations, each testing a specific skill or competency for a fixed time, and are scored by examiners using pre-validated checklists or rating scales.
  • It is "objective" because all students face the same tasks and criteria, and "structured" because the content and scoring are planned in advance.

Types of stations

  1. Procedure (observed) stations – the student performs a task while the examiner observes and scores with a checklist (e.g. measuring blood pressure, hand washing, preparing an injection, CPR on a manikin, interpreting a partograph).
  2. Question (response) stations – the student answers questions in writing about a previous station, a specimen, chart, X-ray, ECG, drug label or case (e.g. calculating a drug dose).
  3. Standardised patient stations – communication, history-taking or counselling with a trained actor.
  4. Rest stations – breaks between stations.

Planning and conduct

  1. Blueprint – select competencies to be tested according to learning outcomes and the domains (skills, knowledge, communication, attitude).
  2. Design stations – clear task instructions for students, checklists with marks for each step, equipment lists, instructions for examiners and standardised patients.
  3. Fix time – usually 3–5 minutes per station (sometimes up to 10), with a signal (bell or timer) to move; the number of stations depends on the competencies (often 10–20).
  4. Set up the area – stations arranged in a circuit with numbers and arrows; equipment ready.
  5. Brief students and examiners.
  6. Conduct – students move from station to station at the signal; examiners observe and score silently.
  7. Compile and analyse scores; give feedback to students.

Advantages

  • Objectivity and reliability – same tasks, standard checklists, many examiners.
  • Tests a wide range of skills in a short time.
  • Reduces examiner bias and patient variability.
  • Assesses communication, attitudes and decision-making as well as procedures.
  • Gives specific feedback for improvement; can be used for formative and summative purposes.
  • Students know exactly what is expected.

Limitations

  • Needs careful planning, time, space, equipment, manpower and trained examiners.
  • Expensive and tiring for examiners.
  • Breaking performance into fragments may not assess holistic patient care (supplement with long cases and workplace assessment).
  • Stress for students due to strict timing; checklist rigidity may miss overall quality.

Example of a procedure station – "Station 4 (5 minutes): Measure the radial pulse of the simulated patient and record it." The checklist includes greeting and explaining the procedure, hand hygiene, correct position and site, counting for one full minute, noting rate, rhythm and volume, informing the patient and recording accurately.

Conclusion OSCE/OSPE assesses clinical and practical competence through timed stations (procedure, question, standardised patient and rest stations) scored with pre-validated checklists; it is objective, reliable and comprehensive but needs planning and resources.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the checklist and the rating scale as tools for clinical evaluation.
answer_html:
1. Checklist

  • Definition – a list of specific behaviours, steps or characteristics that the observer marks as present or absent (yes/no, done/not done) while observing a performance.
  • Construction
    • Analyse the skill into its essential steps in sequence.
    • Write each step as a clear, observable behaviour.
    • Provide columns for "done/not done" and remarks; give marks or weight to critical steps; mark safety-critical steps (e.g. checking patient identity).
  • Uses – evaluating procedures (catheterisation, injection, dressing), OSCE stations, self- and peer-evaluation, ensuring that all steps are followed.
  • Advantages – simple, quick and objective; easy to use by different observers; shows exactly which steps were missed; useful for feedback.
  • Limitations – records only presence or absence, not the quality of performance; a long list can be tedious; may encourage mechanical performance.

2. Rating scale

  • Definition – a tool for judging the degree or quality of a behaviour or characteristic on a scale of values.
  • Types
    • Numerical rating scale – numbers represent levels (e.g. 1 = poor to 5 = excellent).
    • Graphic rating scale – a line with points labelled (always, often, sometimes, rarely, never).
    • Descriptive rating scale – short descriptions of each level of performance.
    • Behaviourally anchored rating scale (BARS) – each level is described by specific examples of behaviour.
  • Construction
    • Identify the qualities to be rated (e.g. knowledge, skill, communication, safety, responsibility, punctuality).
    • Define each clearly; choose the number of points (3–7) and describe each level.
    • Give clear instructions to raters.
  • Uses – clinical evaluation of overall performance, professional behaviour and attitudes; evaluation of presentations, teaching and staff performance.
  • Advantages – measures quality and degree; covers many aspects including attitudes; easy to use and compare.
  • Limitations – rater errors
    • Halo effect.
    • Leniency or severity error.
    • Central tendency error.
    • Logical error (assuming that related traits are equal).
    • Personal bias.
    • These are reduced by clear descriptions, training of raters, multiple raters and observation on several occasions.

Difference in brief – a checklist shows whether a behaviour occurred (yes/no); a rating scale shows how well it was performed (degree).

Conclusion Checklists (yes/no records of essential steps) and rating scales (judgement of the quality of performance on numerical, graphic, descriptive or behaviourally anchored scales) are complementary observation tools; clear construction and trained raters make clinical evaluation fair and useful.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the clinical portfolio, logbook and self-evaluation in nursing education.
answer_html:
1. Clinical portfolio

  • Definition – a purposeful collection of evidence of a student's learning, achievements and professional development over a period of time, with the student's reflections on that learning.
  • Contents
    • Personal profile and learning goals.
    • Clinical experiences and competencies achieved.
    • Nursing care plans, case and care studies, health education plans.
    • Reflective journals and critical incidents.
    • Feedback and evaluations from teachers and staff.
    • Certificates (BLS, workshops, conferences), research or project work, awards.
    • Self-assessment and action plans.
  • Types – paper portfolios and electronic portfolios (e-portfolios); showcase (best work) and developmental (progress over time) portfolios.
  • Assessment – reviewed periodically with a rubric (organisation, evidence of competence, quality of reflection, progress).
  • Advantages – shows growth over time; develops reflection, self-directed and lifelong learning; holistic assessment of knowledge, skills and attitudes; useful for job applications and professional development.
  • Limitations – time-consuming to prepare and assess; subjectivity in assessment; quality varies.

2. Logbook

  • Definition – a record maintained by the student of clinical procedures and experiences, indicating whether each was observed, assisted or performed independently, with the date, the number of times performed and the signature of the supervisor.
  • Uses
    • Ensures that students obtain the required clinical experiences and competencies (the INC curriculum prescribes clinical requirements and competency logbooks for each clinical course).
    • Helps teachers plan clinical assignments to fill gaps.
    • Serves as evidence for eligibility for examinations.
  • Limitations – may become a formality if signatures are given without verifying performance.

3. Self-evaluation (self-assessment)

  • Definition – the process by which students judge their own performance against set criteria and identify strengths, weaknesses and learning needs.
  • Methods – self-rating with checklists and rating scales, reflective journals, reviewing video recordings of their own performance, comparing with standards, discussing with the teacher.
  • Benefits
    • Develops self-awareness, responsibility, reflection and self-directed learning.
    • Motivates improvement; reduces dependence on the teacher.
    • Prepares students for lifelong professional self-regulation.
  • Limitations – students may overrate or underrate themselves; needs guidance and comparison with the teacher's evaluation.

Conclusion The clinical portfolio (a reflective collection of evidence of learning), the logbook (a signed record of procedures observed, assisted and performed) and self-evaluation (judging one's own performance against criteria) together support continuous, competency-based assessment and develop reflective, self-directed nurses.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the characteristics of a good test.
answer_html:
1. Validity

  • Meaning – the extent to which a test measures what it is intended to measure (the most important characteristic).
  • Types
    • Content validity – the test adequately samples the content and objectives (ensured by a blueprint).
    • Construct validity – measures the theoretical trait (e.g. critical thinking).
    • Criterion-related validity – results agree with an external criterion – concurrent (with another test at the same time) or predictive (future performance).
    • Face validity – appears to measure what it should.
  • Factors reducing validity – unclear directions, ambiguous items, items not matching objectives, too difficult vocabulary, inadequate time, cheating.

2. Reliability

  • Meaning – the consistency of test scores – the same results on repeated testing or with different examiners.
  • Methods of estimating – test–retest, parallel (equivalent) forms, split-half (odd–even items) and inter-rater reliability (agreement between examiners).
  • Factors affecting reliability – length of the test (longer tests are more reliable), subjective scoring, ambiguous items, guessing, students' condition, testing conditions.
  • A test can be reliable without being valid, but a valid test must be reliable.

3. Objectivity

  • Scoring is not influenced by the examiner's personal judgement; different examiners give the same score. Achieved by clear items, answer keys, marking schemes and checklists.

4. Usability (practicability)

  • Easy to administer, score and interpret; reasonable in time and cost; clear instructions; available materials.

5. Discriminating power

  • Distinguishes between high and low achievers (measured by the discrimination index).

6. Comprehensiveness and adequacy

  • Covers all important objectives and content; has enough items to sample the area.

7. Appropriate difficulty

  • Neither too easy nor too difficult for the group; a mix of easy, average and difficult items.

8. Clarity and fairness

  • Clear language and directions; free from bias (gender, culture, language); equal opportunity for all.

9. Economy – efficient use of time, effort and resources.

10. Educational value – encourages good study habits and gives useful feedback.

Relationship – objectivity of scoring increases reliability, and a reliable test is a precondition for validity; usability decides whether a good test can actually be used in a particular setting.

Conclusion A good test is valid (content, construct, criterion, face), reliable (consistent across time, forms and examiners), objective, usable, discriminating, comprehensive, of appropriate difficulty, clear and fair, economical and educationally valuable.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the assessment tests for higher learning – interpretive questions, hot spot, drag-and-drop and ordered response items.
answer_html:
Introduction Traditional recall questions do not assess clinical reasoning, analysis and judgement. Alternative and computer-based item formats – increasingly used in licensing examinations – assess higher learning by asking students to interpret data, identify, arrange and prioritise.

1. Interpretive (context-dependent) questions

  • A set of questions based on introductory material – a patient scenario, chart, graph, laboratory report, ECG strip, partograph, drug label or picture.
  • Example – a vital signs chart showing rising pulse and falling BP after surgery, followed by questions: "What is the most likely problem? What is the priority nursing action?"
  • Assesses interpretation, analysis, application and clinical judgement.
  • Construction – realistic, relevant material; questions that require using the material, not just recall; several items per set.

2. Hot spot items

  • The student identifies an area on an image (e.g. a diagram, photograph or anatomical figure) by clicking or marking it.
  • Examples – "Click on the site for intramuscular injection in the ventrogluteal area"; "Mark the point of maximum impulse on the chest"; "Identify the area of a pressure ulcer risk".
  • Assesses application of knowledge of anatomy, landmarks and assessment.

3. Drag-and-drop items

  • The student moves options into the correct boxes or categories (classification, matching or prioritisation).
  • Example – drag the signs into "Hypoglycaemia" or "Hyperglycaemia"; drag nursing actions into "immediate" and "later".
  • Assesses classification, discrimination and prioritisation.

4. Ordered response (sequencing) items

  • The student arranges steps or actions in the correct order.
  • Example – arrange the steps of adult CPR, the steps of donning PPE, or the order of nursing actions for a patient in anaphylaxis.
  • Assesses understanding of procedures and priorities.

5. Other higher-order formats – multiple-response ("select all that apply"), extended matching, case clusters (several questions on an unfolding case), and "bow-tie" or matrix items used to assess clinical judgement.

Advantages

  • Assess higher-order thinking and clinical judgement closer to real practice.
  • Engaging and realistic; computer scoring is objective and quick.
  • Prepare students for computer-based licensing examinations.

Limitations

  • Need computer-based testing facilities and software.
  • Time-consuming to construct and validate; teachers need training.
  • Partial-credit scoring rules must be decided in advance.

Conclusion Interpretive questions, hot spot, drag-and-drop and ordered-response items, along with multiple-response and case-cluster formats, assess interpretation, identification, classification, sequencing and prioritisation – the higher learning and clinical judgement that nurses need.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Define assessment.
answer_html:
Assessment is the systematic process of collecting, analysing and using information about students' learning – their knowledge, skills and attitudes – in order to judge their progress, give feedback and improve learning and teaching.

  • It uses many methods – written tests, practical examinations, observation, assignments, projects, portfolios and self-evaluation.
  • Types – formative assessment (during learning, for feedback – "assessment for learning") and summative assessment (at the end, for grading and certification – "assessment of learning").
  • Assessment differs from evaluation, which adds a value judgement about the worth or quality of the learning or programme.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Differentiate between formative and summative evaluation.
answer_html:
Formative evaluation

  • When – during the course, while learning is going on.
  • Purpose – to monitor progress, give feedback and improve teaching and learning; diagnose difficulties.
  • Examples – class tests, quizzes, assignments, clinical feedback, return demonstrations.

  • Usually low stakes; results are used for remedial action. Summative evaluation

  • When – at the end of a unit, semester or course.

  • Purpose – to judge achievement, grade, certify or promote.
  • Examples – end-semester theory and practical examinations, university examinations.
  • High stakes; results are used for decisions. Both are needed – formative evaluation helps students reach the standards tested in summative evaluation.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: What is a blueprint (table of specifications)?
answer_html: A blueprint (table of specifications) is a two-way chart prepared before constructing a test, showing the distribution of marks or questions across content areas (units/topics) and levels of learning objectives (knowledge, understanding, application), and often by type of question. Steps – list units with their weightage (according to teaching hours or importance), decide the weightage for each level of objectives and question types, and distribute marks in each cell so that the total equals the test's marks. Importance – ensures content validity and balanced coverage; prevents over-emphasis on some topics; guides the paper-setter; makes tests comparable from year to year.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: What is item analysis?
answer_html:
Item analysis is the process of examining students' responses to each test item (especially MCQs) to judge the quality of the items.

  • Difficulty index (P) – the percentage of students who answered the item correctly: P = (H + L) / N × 100, where H and L are the numbers answering correctly in the high- and low-scoring groups and N is the total number in both groups; items of moderate difficulty (about 30–70%) are generally preferred.
  • Discrimination index (D) – how well the item separates high and low achievers: D = (H − L) / n, where n is the number in each group; values of about 0.25 and above indicate good discrimination; negative values indicate a faulty item.
  • Distractor analysis – a good distractor is chosen by some low scorers; distractors chosen by nobody are revised. Item analysis helps improve items and build a question bank.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: (a) Define counselling and differentiate it from guidance. (4 marks) (b) Explain the principles, types and process of counselling. (7 marks) (c) Describe the skills of a counsellor and the organisation of counselling services in a nursing institution. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Stages of the counselling process
labels: establishing rapport and a helping relationship – exploration and assessment of the problem – setting goals together – planning and taking action – termination and follow-up
genuineness and unconditional positive regard throughout

answer_html:
(a) Definition and difference from guidance (4 marks) Definitions

  • Counselling is a professional, confidential helping relationship in which a trained person (counsellor) helps an individual (client) to understand himself or herself, explore problems and feelings, make decisions and solve problems independently.
  • Carl Rogers described counselling as a series of direct contacts with the individual which aims to offer him assistance in changing his attitudes and behaviour.
  • Guidance is a broader process of helping individuals to understand themselves and their opportunities, and to make wise choices, plans and adjustments in educational, vocational and personal matters.

Differences between guidance and counselling

  • Scope – guidance is broad and comprehensive; counselling is a specific, intensive part of guidance ("counselling is the heart of guidance").
  • Nature – guidance is largely preventive and developmental, often informational (giving information about courses, careers, rules); counselling is more remedial and therapeutic, dealing with personal and emotional problems.
  • Approach – guidance is often given to groups and may be directive (advice); counselling is usually individual or small-group, focusing on the person's feelings and self-understanding.
  • Depth – guidance deals with external choices and plans; counselling deals with attitudes, feelings and behaviour change.
  • Provider – guidance can be given by any teacher; counselling needs special training and skills.
  • Confidentiality – essential in counselling.

Objectives of counselling – to help the student gain self-understanding, solve problems, make decisions, cope with stress and crises, develop self-confidence and adjust to the academic, clinical and social environment.

(b) Principles, types and process of counselling (7 marks) Principles

  1. Acceptance – accept the student as a person with dignity and worth.
  2. Respect for the individual and individual differences.
  3. Confidentiality – information is kept private, except when there is danger to life or a legal duty.
  4. Empathy – understand the student's feelings from his or her point of view.
  5. Non-judgemental attitude – no blaming or moralising.
  6. Self-determination – the student makes his or her own decisions.
  7. Genuineness and honesty of the counsellor.
  8. Voluntary participation – counselling cannot be forced.
  9. Client-centredness – focus on the student's needs, not the counsellor's views.
  10. Continuity and follow-up; referral when the problem is beyond the counsellor's competence.

Types of counselling A. By approach

  • Directive (counsellor-centred) counselling – E. G. Williamson; the counsellor analyses the problem and advises; quick, useful for informational and academic problems, but may make the student dependent.
  • Non-directive (client-centred) counselling – Carl Rogers; the counsellor provides a warm, accepting atmosphere and the student finds his or her own solutions; good for emotional problems, but time-consuming.
  • Eclectic counselling – F. C. Thorne; a flexible combination of directive and non-directive methods according to the person and problem. B. By number – individual counselling and group counselling (students with common problems, e.g. examination anxiety, homesickness). C. By area – academic (study skills, poor performance, examinations), career/vocational, personal and emotional, social and family, health-related (stress, substance use), crisis counselling (death of a patient or family member, trauma, suicidal thoughts). D. Others – peer counselling by trained senior students; online/tele-counselling.

Process (stages) of counselling

  1. Establishing rapport (initial disclosure) – a warm welcome, privacy, comfortable seating, explanation of confidentiality; building trust.
  2. Exploration and assessment (in-depth exploration) – the student tells his or her story; the counsellor listens actively, asks open questions and gathers information (background, academic records, health, family).
  3. Identifying the problem and setting goals – clarifying the real problem; setting realistic goals together.
  4. Planning and action (commitment to action) – exploring alternatives and their consequences; the student chooses a course of action; the counsellor supports, teaches skills (time management, relaxation, study skills) and gives information.
  5. Termination – when goals are achieved; summarising progress; preparing the student to manage independently.
  6. Follow-up and evaluation – checking progress and offering further help; referral if needed.

(c) Counselling skills and organisation of services (4 marks) Skills and techniques of counselling

  • Attending – giving full attention with appropriate posture, eye contact and facial expression ("SOLER" – sit squarely, open posture, lean forward, eye contact, relaxed).
  • Active listening – listening to words and feelings without interrupting.
  • Empathy – communicating understanding of feelings.
  • Questioning – open-ended questions to explore; closed questions for specific information.
  • Paraphrasing and reflection of feelings – restating content and feelings to show understanding.
  • Clarification and summarising.
  • Silence – allowing the student time to think and express.
  • Confrontation – gently pointing out inconsistencies.
  • Information giving, reassurance and encouragement.
  • Problem-solving and decision-making support.

Roles of the counsellor – listener, helper, guide, educator, motivator, advocate, liaison with parents and authorities, referral agent and record keeper.

Organisation of counselling services in a nursing institution

  • A Guidance and Counselling Cell with a trained counsellor (or faculty with counselling training) and a coordinator.
  • Mentor (faculty adviser) system – each faculty member is assigned a small group of students for academic advising and personal support throughout the course.
  • A private, comfortable counselling room and fixed hours; confidentiality of records.
  • Orientation programmes for new students; workshops on study skills, stress management and life skills.
  • Peer support and peer-counselling programmes.
  • Coordination with the anti-ragging committee, grievance redressal committee, women's cell and hostel wardens.
  • Referral links with psychiatrists, psychologists, medical officers and Tele-MANAS.
  • Records, periodic reports and evaluation of services.

Counselling needs of nursing students – adjustment to a new environment and hostel life, homesickness, academic difficulties, language problems, heavy workload, fear and stress in clinical areas, exposure to suffering and death, examination anxiety, financial and family problems, relationship issues, ragging or harassment, health problems, career choices.

Example of a counselling interaction (brief) – a second-year student who failed a test and has stopped attending clinical duty is called by her mentor. In a private room, the teacher greets her warmly, assures confidentiality and asks, "You seem worried these days – would you like to talk about it?" The student shares that her father is ill and she is anxious about fees. The teacher listens, reflects her feelings ("You are carrying a lot of worry for your family"), helps her list options (scholarship, talking to the principal about fee instalments, a study plan), and they agree on steps. A follow-up meeting is fixed after one week.

Ethical aspects of counselling – confidentiality, informed consent for any referral, avoiding dual relationships that affect objectivity (e.g. counselling a student while also deciding her marks in a dispute), respecting the student's values, and recognising the limits of one's competence.

Conclusion Counselling is a confidential, professional helping relationship that enables a student to understand and solve personal problems; it is a specific, intensive part of the broader, largely informational and preventive process of guidance. It is based on principles of acceptance, confidentiality, empathy, a non-judgemental attitude and self-determination; it may be directive, non-directive or eclectic, individual or group, academic, career, personal or crisis-related; and it follows stages from rapport through exploration, goal setting and action to termination and follow-up. Counselling skills such as attending, active listening, empathy, questioning, paraphrasing, reflection and summarising, along with an organised counselling cell, mentor system and referral links, help nursing students cope with their many academic, clinical and personal challenges.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the principles of guidance.
answer_html:
Definition Guidance is the process of helping individuals to understand themselves and their environment, so that they can make wise choices, plans and adjustments in their educational, vocational and personal lives.

Objectives

  • To help students know their abilities, interests and limitations.
  • To help them adjust to the institution, hostel and clinical environment.
  • To help in educational and career planning.
  • To promote personal, social and emotional development.
  • To prevent problems and to identify students needing counselling.

Scope (types of guidance) – educational guidance (choice of courses, study habits, examinations), vocational/career guidance (job opportunities, higher studies, specialisations, nursing abroad), personal and social guidance (adjustment, relationships, health and stress).

Principles of guidance

  1. Guidance is for all students – not only for those with problems.
  2. Guidance is a continuous process – throughout the course, from admission to placement.
  3. Respect for the individual – every student has dignity and worth.
  4. Individual differences – guidance is based on each student's abilities, interests and needs.
  5. Holistic approach – concerned with the whole personality (intellectual, emotional, social, physical).
  6. Self-direction – helps students to make their own decisions; does not impose decisions.
  7. Cooperative effort – involves teachers, parents, counsellors, administrators and the student.
  8. Based on accurate information – about the student (records, tests) and about opportunities.
  9. Flexibility – adapts to changing needs of students and society.
  10. Preventive and developmental emphasis rather than only remedial.
  11. Confidentiality of personal information.
  12. Evaluation – the guidance programme should be evaluated periodically.
  13. Trained personnel – guidance should be given by persons with appropriate knowledge and attitude.

Roles of faculty in guidance

  • Act as mentors and academic advisers to a group of students.
  • Observe students and identify difficulties early.
  • Give information about rules, courses, careers and higher education.
  • Maintain cumulative records; involve parents when necessary.
  • Refer students to the counsellor when needed.

Conclusion Guidance helps students understand themselves and make wise educational, vocational and personal choices; it is guided by principles such as being for all, continuous, respectful of individuality and individual differences, holistic, self-directing, cooperative, information-based, flexible, preventive, confidential and evaluated, with faculty playing key roles as mentors and advisers.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain discipline among nursing students and the management of disciplinary problems.
answer_html:
Meaning

  • Discipline is the orderly conduct of individuals according to accepted rules and values, which enables effective learning and professional behaviour.
  • In nursing, discipline is essential for patient safety, teamwork and the image of the profession.
  • The aim is self-discipline – control from within – rather than imposed discipline through fear.

Common disciplinary problems – irregular attendance, late coming to class or duty, improper uniform, mobile phone misuse, disrespect to teachers or staff, absence from clinical duties without permission, unprofessional behaviour with patients, cheating and plagiarism, ragging, violation of hostel rules, substance use, misuse of social media (sharing patient photos).

Causes of indiscipline

  • Student factors – lack of interest or motivation, stress, family and financial problems, peer pressure, immaturity, health problems.
  • Teacher factors – poor teaching, inconsistency, favouritism, harsh or humiliating behaviour, poor role modelling.
  • Institutional factors – unclear or rigid rules, poor facilities, heavy workload, lack of communication and grievance channels.
  • Social factors – changing values, media influence.

Preventive measures (preventive guidance and counselling)

  • Clear code of conduct explained at orientation and in the student handbook.
  • Good teaching and positive role models; fair and consistent application of rules.
  • Mentor system and regular communication with students and parents.
  • Student participation in decision-making (student nurses' association, class representatives).
  • Co-curricular activities for constructive use of energy.
  • Early identification of problems and counselling; stress management programmes.
  • Grievance redressal mechanisms, an anti-ragging committee and a women's grievance cell.

Managing disciplinary problems Principles

  • Deal with problems promptly, privately and calmly.
  • Find the cause before acting.
  • Be fair and consistent; follow natural justice – give the student a chance to explain (right to be heard).
  • Corrective rather than punitive; the penalty should be proportionate.
  • Maintain confidentiality and records. Steps
  1. Informal discussion with the student – listening, understanding the cause, counselling.
  2. Verbal warning and agreement on expected behaviour.
  3. Written warning; informing parents or guardians.
  4. Reference to the disciplinary committee for serious or repeated misconduct – inquiry, hearing, decision.
  5. Disciplinary action as per rules – fine, suspension from hostel or classes, or, in serious cases such as ragging, expulsion (according to the regulations on curbing ragging).
  6. Follow-up and support for improvement.

Role of the teacher – role model of punctuality and professional conduct; maintains a positive climate; identifies problems early; counsels; applies rules fairly; documents incidents; communicates with authorities.

Conclusion Discipline among nursing students aims at self-discipline and professional conduct; indiscipline arises from student, teacher, institutional and social causes. It is best prevented through a clear code of conduct, good role models, mentoring, participation, activities, counselling and grievance mechanisms, and managed promptly, fairly and correctively, following natural justice and graded steps.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: Explain the counselling needs of nursing students and the role of the faculty.
answer_html:
Introduction Nursing students face unique pressures – long hours, demanding clinical work, exposure to suffering and responsibility for patients – in addition to the usual problems of young adults. Many are away from home for the first time. Identifying and meeting their counselling needs is an important responsibility of the institution.

Common counselling needs

  1. Adjustment problems – new environment, hostel life, homesickness, food, language and cultural differences, making friends.
  2. Academic problems – difficulty with English or science subjects, heavy curriculum, poor study habits, failure in examinations, examination anxiety.
  3. Clinical stress – fear of making mistakes, first experiences of procedures, night duties, conflicts with staff, feeling unsupported.
  4. Emotional impact of patient care – exposure to pain, death and dying, violence and abuse cases; compassion fatigue.
  5. Personal and family problems – illness or death in the family, financial difficulties, family pressure regarding marriage, relationship problems.
  6. Health problems – physical illness, menstrual problems, sleep disturbance, depression and anxiety, eating problems, substance use.
  7. Ragging, bullying, harassment and discrimination.
  8. Career-related concerns – choice of specialisation, higher studies, job opportunities in India and abroad, competitive examinations.
  9. Social media and technology-related problems – cyber-bullying, internet addiction.

Identifying students who need counselling

  • Sudden fall in academic performance or attendance.
  • Withdrawal, irritability, frequent crying, changes in appetite or sleep.
  • Frequent illness complaints; late coming; disciplinary problems.
  • Expressions of hopelessness or self-harm – requires immediate attention and referral.
  • Information from friends, hostel wardens and clinical staff.

Role of the faculty

  • Mentor/academic adviser – meet assigned students regularly; know their background and progress.
  • Create an approachable, supportive atmosphere; listen without judging.
  • Provide academic help – remedial classes, study skills, peer tutoring.
  • Support in the clinical area – orientation, gradual responsibility, debriefing after distressing events.
  • Teach coping skills – time management, relaxation, yoga, stress management.
  • Maintain confidentiality, but act immediately when there is danger to life.
  • Refer to the counsellor, medical officer, psychiatrist or Tele-MANAS as needed; involve parents when appropriate.
  • Prevent ragging and harassment; inform students about grievance mechanisms.
  • Career guidance – information about higher education, specialisation and job opportunities.
  • Keep records and evaluate the effectiveness of help given.

Conclusion Nursing students need counselling for adjustment, academic, clinical, emotional, personal, health, safety and career concerns. Faculty, especially as mentors, help by recognising warning signs early, offering a supportive relationship, academic and clinical support, coping skills, confidentiality, timely referral and career guidance.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: What is a grievance redressal cell? State its functions.
answer_html:
A grievance redressal cell (committee) is a body set up in an educational institution to receive and resolve complaints (grievances) of students in a fair, confidential and time-bound manner.

  • The UGC (Redressal of Grievances of Students) Regulations, 2023 require every higher education institution to have a Students' Grievance Redressal Committee (SGRC), with an Ombudsperson at university level to hear appeals. Functions

  • Receive grievances about admissions, fees, examinations and evaluation, attendance, scholarships, facilities, harassment and discrimination.

  • Inquire into complaints, hear both sides and recommend solutions within a fixed time.
  • Maintain confidentiality and protect students from victimisation.
  • Inform students about the procedure; keep records and report to the authorities.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
question: List the techniques of counselling.
answer_html:
Techniques (approaches)

  1. Directive (counsellor-centred) – the counsellor analyses the problem and advises (E. G. Williamson).
  2. Non-directive (client-centred) – the counsellor creates an accepting atmosphere and the client finds the solution (Carl Rogers).
  3. Eclectic – a flexible combination of both (F. C. Thorne). Skills used in counselling
  • Attending and active listening.
  • Empathy.
  • Open-ended questioning.
  • Paraphrasing, reflection of feelings, clarification and summarising.
  • Use of silence; gentle confrontation.
  • Information giving, reassurance and encouragement.
  • Problem-solving and support in decision-making.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
unit_title: Ethics and Evidence-based Teaching in Nursing Education
question: (a) Explain the ethical principles applied to nursing education. (5 marks) (b) Describe the ethical considerations in nursing education – for teachers, students, clinical teaching, assessment and research. (10 marks)

diagram.caption: Ethical relationships in nursing education
labels: the patient and the institution connected by duties of respect
framed by the INC code of ethics and institutional policies

answer_html:
(a) Ethical principles applied to nursing education (5 marks) Ethics is the branch of philosophy that deals with moral principles of right and wrong conduct. In nursing education, ethics guides the relationships and actions of teachers, students and institutions, as well as the care of patients used for teaching.

  1. Respect for persons and autonomy
    • Respecting the dignity, rights and opinions of students and patients.
    • Allowing students to make choices within rules (e.g. electives, self-directed learning).
    • Obtaining patients' consent before students care for or examine them.
  2. Beneficence – acting in the best interests of students (good teaching, guidance, support) and of patients (quality care).
  3. Non-maleficence – avoiding harm – to patients (by unsafe student practice) and to students (humiliation, harassment, unfair evaluation, exploitation).
  4. Justice (fairness)
    • Equal treatment of all students irrespective of caste, religion, gender, economic status or region.
    • Fair allocation of clinical experiences.
    • Fair and transparent assessment.
  5. Veracity (truthfulness) – honesty in teaching, feedback, evaluation, records and research.
  6. Fidelity – keeping promises and commitments; loyalty to the profession and the institution.
  7. Confidentiality – protecting students' personal information, marks and counselling records, and patients' information used in teaching.
  8. Accountability and integrity – responsibility for one's actions and maintaining professional standards.

(b) Ethical considerations in nursing education (10 marks) 1. Ethical responsibilities of the teacher

  • Competence – maintain updated knowledge and teaching and clinical skills; teach only what one is competent to teach.
  • Fairness and impartiality – no favouritism or discrimination; equal opportunities to learn.
  • Respect – treat students with dignity; never humiliate, insult or abuse them, especially in front of patients and staff.
  • Professional boundaries – avoid exploitation, inappropriate relationships, accepting gifts or favours that affect objectivity, or using students for personal work.
  • Honest feedback and evaluation – timely, constructive and based on evidence.
  • Role modelling – demonstrate ethical conduct, punctuality, caring and integrity.
  • Academic honesty – credit sources, avoid plagiarism in one's own teaching material and publications.
  • Confidentiality of student information.
  • Academic freedom with responsibility – presenting content objectively, including different viewpoints.
  • Student welfare – attention to safety, health and well-being; preventing ragging and harassment.

2. Students' rights and responsibilities

  • Rights – to quality education and adequate clinical experience; to fair and transparent evaluation; to be informed of rules and criteria; to privacy; to freedom from discrimination, ragging and harassment; to express grievances and be heard (grievance redressal).
