  • Responsibilities – to attend regularly and be punctual; to prepare and participate; to follow the code of conduct; to maintain academic integrity (no cheating, plagiarism, falsification of records or logbooks); to practise safely within their level of competence; to respect patients, teachers, staff and peers; to protect patient confidentiality.

3. Ethics in clinical teaching

  • Patient safety first – students perform procedures only after learning them in the skill lab and under supervision; they must not exceed their competence.
  • Informed consent of patients – patients should know that a student is involved and may refuse without affecting their care.
  • Privacy and dignity – limiting the number of students at the bedside; covering patients; discussing sensitive matters away from the bedside.
  • Confidentiality – patient information used in care studies and presentations is de-identified; no photographs or sharing on social media.
  • Vulnerable patients (unconscious, children, mentally ill, poor) must not be used merely as teaching material.
  • Honest documentation – students record only what they did.
  • Reporting errors – a culture where students can report mistakes without fear, so that patients are protected and learning occurs.

4. Ethics in assessment

  • Validity, reliability and fairness – tests match objectives; criteria known in advance.
  • Confidentiality of question papers and results; prevention of leakage and malpractice.
  • Objectivity – avoid bias; use model answers and checklists; double valuation where possible.
  • Timely feedback and opportunity for revaluation or appeal.
  • Avoid misuse of internal assessment marks as a tool of control or punishment.

5. Ethics in research and scholarly work

  • Informed consent, voluntary participation, confidentiality and protection from harm for participants (including students as participants – they should not feel coerced).
  • Approval of the institutional ethics committee; following national ethical guidelines (ICMR).
  • Honesty – no fabrication, falsification or plagiarism; proper authorship and acknowledgement.

6. Institutional ethics

  • Transparent admission and fee policies; adequate facilities and qualified faculty as per regulatory norms.
  • Grievance redressal, anti-ragging and anti-harassment mechanisms.
  • Safe working and learning environment; ethical use of technology and student data.

7. Ethical decision-making in nursing education

  • When dilemmas arise (e.g. a student caught copying, a teacher asked to change marks, a patient refusing student care), the teacher identifies the facts and values involved, considers the alternatives and their consequences, consults policies and colleagues, decides and acts, and then evaluates the outcome.

Common ethical issues in nursing education

  • Academic dishonesty – copying in examinations, plagiarism in assignments, signing attendance for others, completing logbooks without performing procedures.
  • Students working beyond their competence because of staff shortage in wards.
  • Unfair evaluation – bias, favouritism, using internal marks to punish or reward.
  • Harassment and ragging; humiliation of students in front of patients.
  • Breach of confidentiality – discussing patients or students in public places or on social media.
  • Conflicts of interest – private tuition by teachers to their own students, accepting gifts.
  • Use of students as cheap labour rather than learners.
  • Pressure on faculty to pass students who are not competent, which endangers patients.

Role of the code of ethics and policies – the INC code of ethics and professional conduct, the institution's code of conduct for faculty and students, anti-ragging rules and grievance procedures provide a framework; teachers should explain these to students at orientation and apply them consistently.

Ethical teaching of ethics – ethics is best taught not only through lectures but through discussion of real dilemmas, reflection and, above all, the example of teachers who show honesty, fairness and respect in everyday interactions with students and patients.

Ethics in online and digital teaching – recording lectures and online classes only with consent; protecting students' personal data and examination records; ensuring fairness when some students lack devices or internet; preventing cyber-bullying in class groups; using licensed or open materials and acknowledging sources; and setting clear rules for the use of artificial intelligence tools in assignments.

Professional accountability of nurse educators – teachers are accountable to students (for quality teaching and fair evaluation), to patients (for the safety of care given by students), to the profession and regulatory bodies (for maintaining standards) and to society (for producing competent, ethical nurses). Ethical conduct by educators therefore protects not only students but also the public.

Conclusion Ethical principles – respect for persons and autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, veracity, fidelity, confidentiality and accountability – guide nursing education. They require teachers to be competent, fair, respectful, honest role models who maintain boundaries and confidentiality; students to uphold academic integrity and safe, respectful practice; clinical teaching to protect patient safety, consent, privacy and confidentiality; assessment to be valid, fair and confidential; research to follow consent and integrity; and institutions to provide transparent, safe and just environments.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
unit_title: Ethics and Evidence-based Teaching in Nursing Education
question: Explain the student–faculty relationship in nursing education.
answer_html:
Meaning The student–faculty relationship is the professional, educational relationship between teachers and students that develops through teaching, clinical supervision, mentoring and other interactions. It greatly influences students' learning, motivation, professional socialisation and well-being.

Characteristics of a good student–faculty relationship

  1. Mutual respect and trust – each values the other's dignity and contribution.
  2. Open, two-way communication – students feel free to ask questions, express difficulties and give feedback.
  3. Caring and support – the teacher shows genuine concern for students' learning and well-being.
  4. Fairness and consistency – equal treatment of all; no favouritism.
  5. Professional boundaries – friendly but not overly familiar; no exploitation or inappropriate relationships; confidentiality maintained.
  6. Role modelling – the teacher demonstrates professional values and behaviour.
  7. Partnership in learning – shared responsibility; the teacher facilitates and the student takes initiative.
  8. Constructive feedback – given honestly and respectfully.

Factors affecting the relationship

  • Teacher's personality, attitude and teaching style; workload and time available.
  • Students' attitudes, motivation and background; generation differences.
  • Class size; institutional culture and hierarchy; clinical pressures.
  • Communication skills; language and cultural differences.

Barriers – authoritarian attitudes, humiliation and criticism in public, favouritism, poor communication, unavailability of teachers, mistrust, excessive informality (including social-media familiarity), and stress in clinical settings.

Ways to improve the relationship

  • Mentor/adviser system with regular meetings.
  • Learning students' names and backgrounds; being available and approachable.
  • Active listening and empathy; respecting students' opinions.
  • Clear expectations and fair, transparent evaluation.
  • Positive reinforcement and constructive, private correction.
  • Involving students in decisions (class representatives, feedback on teaching).
  • Joint co-curricular activities.
  • Maintaining professional conduct on and off campus, including online.

Outcomes of a good relationship – better learning and academic performance, motivation, confidence, reduced stress and dropout, development of professional identity and caring behaviour (students treat patients as they are treated), and a positive institutional climate.

Online interactions – teachers should communicate with students through official groups and platforms, avoid private late-night messaging, and not share or comment on students' personal social-media content.

Conclusion A good student–faculty relationship is built on mutual respect, trust, open communication, caring, fairness, professional boundaries and role modelling; strengthened through mentoring, availability, active listening and fair evaluation, it improves learning, well-being and professional development.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
unit_title: Ethics and Evidence-based Teaching in Nursing Education
question: Explain value-based education in nursing.
answer_html:
Meaning

  • Values are beliefs and ideals about what is good, right and desirable, which guide a person's choices and behaviour.
  • Value-based education is education that deliberately develops good human and professional values along with knowledge and skills, so that learners become ethical, responsible and caring individuals and professionals.

Need in nursing

  • Nursing is a caring profession in which patients are vulnerable and trust nurses with their lives and dignity.
  • Rapid technological change, commercialisation of health care and stress can erode values.
  • Ethical dilemmas in practice require a strong value base.
  • Society expects nurses to be compassionate, honest and just; the National Education Policy 2020 also emphasises value-based education.

Core values to be developed

  • Human dignity – respect for every person.
  • Integrity – honesty, truthfulness, keeping promises.
  • Altruism – concern for others' welfare.
  • Autonomy – respecting patients' right to make choices.
  • Social justice – fair and equal care for all.
  • Caring and compassion, responsibility and accountability, confidentiality.
  • Teamwork and respect for colleagues.
  • Commitment to excellence and lifelong learning.
  • Human values – non-violence, tolerance, patriotism, gender equality, environmental care.

Methods of value-based education

  1. Role modelling by teachers and clinical staff – the most powerful method.
  2. Integration of values into all courses – e.g. discussing dignity while teaching bed bath, justice while teaching health programmes.
  3. Ethical case discussions and dilemmas – analysing real situations (refusal of treatment, end-of-life care, confidentiality).
  4. Value clarification exercises – helping students identify and examine their own values (choosing freely, prizing and acting on values).
  5. Reflective journals and critical incident analysis.
  6. Role play, simulation and storytelling – patients' narratives to develop empathy.
  7. Service learning and community activities – health camps, visits to old-age homes, orphanages and leprosy colonies.
  8. Oath-taking ceremonies, code of ethics, celebrations (Nurses' Day, Florence Nightingale's legacy).
  9. A positive institutional culture (hidden curriculum) – fairness, respect and honesty in daily life.
  10. Recognition of students who show exemplary values.

Role of the teacher – be a consistent role model, create a respectful climate, include value-related objectives, discuss values openly, give feedback on professional behaviour and protect students from negative influences.

Evaluation – observation of behaviour with rating scales and anecdotal records, reflective writing, attitude scales and feedback from patients and staff.

Conclusion Value-based education develops human and professional values – dignity, integrity, altruism, autonomy, social justice, caring and accountability – through role modelling, integration in teaching, ethical case discussions, value clarification, reflection, role play, service learning and a positive institutional culture, producing ethical and compassionate nurses.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
unit_title: Ethics and Evidence-based Teaching in Nursing Education
question: Explain evidence-based teaching in nursing education.
answer_html:
Definition Evidence-based teaching (EBT) is the conscientious use of the best available research evidence about teaching and learning, combined with the teacher's expertise and the needs, values and context of learners, to make decisions about teaching methods, curriculum and assessment. It applies the principles of evidence-based practice to education. The Best Evidence Medical and Health Professional Education (BEME) collaboration promotes this approach in health professions education.

Sources of evidence

  • Research studies – randomised trials, quasi-experiments, systematic reviews and meta-analyses in education.
  • Educational evaluation data – student performance, feedback, examination results.
  • Expert consensus, guidelines and the teacher's own reflective experience.

Steps of evidence-based teaching (5 As)

  1. Ask – frame a clear question about a teaching problem (e.g. "Does simulation improve second-year students' competence in managing a deteriorating patient compared with lectures alone?").
  2. Acquire – search for evidence in journals and databases.
  3. Appraise – critically evaluate the quality and relevance of the evidence.
  4. Apply – integrate the evidence with expertise and learners' context in planning teaching.
  5. Assess – evaluate the outcomes (learning, performance, satisfaction) and modify.

Examples of evidence-supported strategies

  • Active learning (PBL, TBL, case-based learning) improves understanding and application.
  • Simulation with structured debriefing improves clinical skills, confidence and teamwork.
  • Timely, specific feedback strongly improves learning.
  • Retrieval practice (frequent low-stakes quizzes) and spaced practice improve long-term retention.
  • Flipped and blended learning support preparation and in-class application.
  • Reflective practice develops clinical reasoning.
  • OSCE and checklists improve the reliability of skill assessment.

Advantages

  • More effective and efficient teaching; better student outcomes.
  • Moves teaching from tradition and habit to rational decisions.
  • Models evidence-based practice for students.
  • Supports curriculum development and accreditation.

Barriers

  • Lack of time, research skills and access to journals.
  • Resistance to change and preference for traditional methods.
  • Limited educational research in the local context.
  • Lack of resources (simulators, technology) to apply findings.

Facilitators – faculty development in research and education, institutional support, journal clubs, collaboration, access to databases and a culture of inquiry.

Role of the nurse teacher – keep updated through reading and conferences, evaluate own teaching systematically, conduct and use educational research, share findings with colleagues and teach students the principles of evidence-based practice.

Conclusion Evidence-based teaching integrates the best research evidence with teacher expertise and learner context through the steps ask, acquire, appraise, apply and assess; using proven strategies such as active learning, simulation with debriefing, feedback, retrieval and spaced practice, it makes nursing education more effective despite barriers of time, skills and resources.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
unit_title: Ethics and Evidence-based Teaching in Nursing Education
question: What are the ethical standards for nursing students?
answer_html:
Ethical standards for nursing students are the principles of conduct that students must follow in academic and clinical settings:

  1. Academic integrity – honesty in examinations, assignments and records; no cheating, plagiarism or falsification of logbooks and attendance.
  2. Respect for patients – dignity, privacy, cultural sensitivity and non-discrimination.
  3. Confidentiality – no disclosure of patient information, including on social media (no photos of patients).
  4. Safe practice – work within one's level of competence, under supervision; report errors honestly.
  5. Professional behaviour – punctuality, proper uniform, courtesy, responsibility and accountability.
  6. Respect for teachers, staff and peers; no ragging or harassment.
  7. Following the code of ethics for nurses and institutional rules.

subject: Educational Technology / Nursing Education
unit_title: Ethics and Evidence-based Teaching in Nursing Education
question: What is plagiarism? How can it be prevented?
answer_html:
Plagiarism is presenting someone else's words, ideas, data or work as one's own without proper acknowledgement. It is a serious breach of academic integrity. Forms – copying text from books or the internet, copying another student's assignment, paraphrasing too closely without citation, buying or outsourcing assignments, reusing one's own previous work without permission (self-plagiarism), and submitting AI-generated text as one's own work where not permitted. Prevention

  • Teach students how to cite and reference (e.g. APA or Vancouver style) and how to paraphrase and summarise properly.
  • Give assignments that require personal reflection and application.
  • Use plagiarism-detection software; follow institutional policies.
  • Explain the consequences (rejection of work, disciplinary action) and promote a culture of honesty.
